text: Midnight: desk booking for Wednesday opens. By 12:01 the only desk left is the one under the hurricane-grade AC. Take it?
The team lead declared Wednesday an “anchor day”: everyone in the office. Only you and he showed up. Everyone else is “anchoring” from home with a fever. Now what?
9:15. Artyom writes: “Hi.” That’s it. Three minutes of silence. Typing… stops… typing again. Reply first?
Vera: “Quick question!” The question turns out to be about the entire project architecture since 2019. Answer in text or hop on a call?
right: Ask her to file a ticket

text: Your first office day in a month. Your badge doesn’t work: the system thinks you quit. The security guard looks at you with pity.
left: Wait in the lobby for a fix

text: Half the team is in the meeting room, half online. Everyone in the room is laughing; the remote folks hear only a muffled roar. Ask them to repeat?
left: Ask them to repeat the joke

text: Colleagues in the meeting room are drawing a diagram on the whiteboard. The camera shows it at an angle, and all you see is glare. Admit you can’t see?
10:00, you’re on a call. Mom calls: “You’re home anyway, pop to the market, the cottage cheese is good today.” Your boss is in the little square on screen.
Mid-call, the intercom buzzes: a courier with your wardrobe. Without you, he’ll leave it outside the building. Your camera is on.
The cat has settled on your warm laptop and won’t let you near the keyboard. Department demo at 1 p.m. The cat is heavy and principled.
right: Run the demo with the cat in shot

text: Morning at the coworking space. The only phone booth is taken by a guy who apparently lives there. Your call starts in five minutes.
Four hours working from the café on a single cappuccino. The barista wipes your table very meaningfully. Order something else?
Working from the country house. There’s signal only on the shed roof. Important client call at 2 p.m. The ladder wobbles.
10 a.m. for you is 5 p.m. for your colleague in the Far East. He writes: “Heading out, reply before my morning.” Your morning is his night.
The calendar said the call was at 3 p.m. — 3 p.m. in another time zone, two hours earlier than yours. Everyone’s been waiting for two hours.
6:30 p.m. Eight straight hours of calls. Square eyes, voice gone. Friends want a video chat. One more screen?
The boss asks you to “give him a quick ring” instead of texting. Half an hour into the call, it turns out it all would’ve fit in one message.
right: Get used to it, say nothing

text: 7:40 p.m. Someone in the team chat asks: “Anyone alive?” You’re alive, but already on the couch. Admit it?
Hybrid day. You arrive to find someone’s mug, blanket and a ficus on your “assigned” desk. The ficus owner arrives at lunch.
HR is running an online team quiz. Cameras mandatory, 10 seconds per question. Your report is on fire.
Your roommate works remotely too. You both have calls at 10:00, and there’s only one quiet room. He’s already carrying a chair in there.
You’re presenting the project, and off-camera your kettle starts whistling. It sounds like a plane taking off.
8:45. Baron demands a walk, and stand-up is at 9:00. Baron stands by the door, leash in mouth, radiating reproach.
You asked a question in the main channel. An hour later: zero replies, six “eyes” reactions and one shrug. Is that an answer?
Your laptop overheated on a pillow and shut down mid stand-up. The bed admits its guilt but won’t give you up.
right: Cool the laptop with a fan

text: 7 p.m. Hybrid day done, you’re heading home. The driver explains he works from his car and is “remote too.” Listen?
Every outlet in the coworking space is taken, and your laptop is at 9%. The guy next to you has three chargers and one phone.
A colleague from across the world writes “Good morning!” at 2 p.m. your time. A minute later: “Why isn’t anything ready yet?”
Morning call, twelve people. Everyone’s camera is off except yours. You’re waving alone into the void.
right: Stay the hero of the screen

text: The AI note-taker summed up the meeting: “Decided: employee (you) takes on everything.” You said no such thing. The notes already went to the boss.
Your cousin: “You work from home, so you’re free — help me move at 7 p.m.” Your deadline is tomorrow morning.
The team lead introduced “async Mondays”: no calls. At 9:30 he writes: “Got five minutes for a quick voice chat?”
The “Library” virtual background cuts off your hand every time you gesture. Colleagues are betting on how many fingers you’ll have left.
left: Turn it off, reveal the mess

text: Office on a Friday. You’re the only one on the floor. The guard asks if you got the day wrong and offers you some tea.
Stas answers everything with stickers. To “Will we make it by Friday?” he sent a dancing raccoon. Is that a yes or a no?
8 p.m. The laptop sits on the kitchen table. You walk past it for the fifth time, and it stares silently. Open it “just for a minute”?
A child on the call loudly announces: “Mommy said this man is going to talk for ages again.” The man is your director.
9 a.m. Messenger, email, tracker, two chats and the corporate portal are all glowing with red numbers. Where to start?
Hybrid Tuesday: everyone came in at once. The microwave queue is twenty people long, plus your buckwheat.
Evening at the country house, laptop on the porch. Mosquitoes attack, and the client wants “one more tiny call.” The porch light draws every mosquito in the county.
Office day today. After two weeks remote, the 7 a.m. alarm feels like a personal insult. Push it to 7:30?
Dima from the next department is DMing you snarky comments about the speaker during the call. The speaker is your boss.
Before your first call you see yourself in the camera preview. Your hair looks like it survived a hurricane. One minute to go.
The “Random Coffee” bot matched you with the CFO for 30 minutes of “just chatting.” Canceling now would be awkward.
Your friend: “You sit at home all day, let’s go for a walk!” You’ve sat on calls all day and want nothing but silence.
The plumber arrives to fix the tap right at stand-up time. He works loudly and narrates every pipe.
Your connection drops mid-sentence. When you’re back, everyone’s on a new topic and you’ve been made the owner of something.
Your phone reports: “Screen time today: 14 hours.” Not counting the laptop. Time to put it all in a drawer?
left: Put the phone in a drawer

text: HR asks you to mark your office days in a spreadsheet. Everyone picked Wednesday, nobody picked Friday. To be fair, they need a volunteer.
Your coworking neighbor is filming for his blog and asks you to “keep it down, I’m doing a take.” You’re at work; he’s on air.
10:30 p.m. A colleague on the other side of the country cheerfully writes: “Good morning! Got twenty minutes for a call?” Your eyes are closing.
6:30 p.m. Your desk is the kitchen table. The family wants dinner, but you’ve got three spreadsheets open and a call in half an hour.
You bought a ring light for calls. In the evening it’s so bright the neighbors across the street drew their curtains. Keep it for tomorrow’s demo?
9:15 p.m. The boss reacts with a “fire” emoji to your message from three hours ago. Is that praise or an emergency? Ask?
Your partner says: “Not a word to me all day, but eight hours of talking to the laptop.” The laptop beeps: new message.
7 p.m. Online office party: everyone at home with a glass of juice, watching the host play guitar. For an hour now. Slip out quietly?
8 p.m. The coworking space is closing; the admin is switching off lights zone by zone. You have two paragraphs of the report left.
The delivery guy rings the doorbell exactly as you say “And now, the final slide.” Camera’s on, the courier is persistent.
right: Let him wait for the slide

text: 6:05 p.m. A colleague writes: “Quick question, but it can wait till tomorrow.” Now you’ll spend all evening wondering what it is. Ask?
Friday, 6 p.m. You’re already at the country house, but the only Wi-Fi is in the sauna. The boss wants the presentation. The sauna’s nicely heated.
Your downstairs neighbor complains you “pace back and forth all day.” That’s you walking during calls to stay awake.
7:30 p.m. You haven’t left the house all day. The step counter says 312 steps, 200 of them to the fridge. Go for a walk?
right: Finish the task on the couch

text: You’re cooking dinner when a colleague video-calls “for a sec.” The pan sizzles, the onions burn, and the colleague sees it all.
8 p.m. Oleg sends a doc “to look at whenever.” Signature: “Whenever = by morning would be nice.” Request or order?
All day on a kitchen chair. Your back announces that starting tomorrow it refuses to work. Order a proper office chair?
left: Buy one with your own money

text: You’re already in bed, and the work messenger on your phone buzzes for the third time. Delete the app from your personal phone?
The boss asks you to listen to his audio recording of “ideas for the week” — 47 minutes. He says it replaces the Monday meeting.
Hybrid Wednesday’s over. Colleagues invite you to a bar — “we rarely see each other in person.” Tomorrow it’s remote again with an early call.
Your kid wants help with homework, but you’re still on a call. The kid sits down next to you and whispers math questions.
The smart speaker heard “reschedule the meeting” on your call and rescheduled your dentist appointment. Trust the speaker?
The power goes out in the evening. The laptop has an hour of battery; the router died instantly. The report is due at 8 p.m.
Your neighbor works from his garage. He invites you over to “see the dream office” — with a barbecue.
6 p.m. for you, 10 p.m. for a colleague four time zones east. She sends a yawning emoji and asks to go through a document together. Now.
HR launched evening online yoga for staff. Cameras mandatory, and your yoga mat is a blanket on the kitchen floor.
Friday evening. You set the auto-reply “Offline until Monday.” A minute later the boss replies to the auto-reply: “Great. But one more thing.”
Timur writes at 8 a.m.: “You online?” You’re in pajamas, coffee isn’t ready, and the green “online” dot has already betrayed you.
right: Go offline for half an hour

text: Hybrid day. You board the train, open the laptop, and the internet drops between every station. Call at 9:30.
5:30 a.m. The neighbor’s rooster has decided you’ll oversleep your call. The call is in four hours.
Grandma video-calls at 9:55 to say she’s watched the weather forecast. Stand-up is at 10:00, and the department head is already on screen.
After a month remote, you open your office locker. It smells of a banana forgotten last quarter.
Hot desk at the office: there’s a monitor, but the port doesn’t fit your laptop. The adapters are with IT, who’s working remotely.
Stand-up: everyone takes turns saying “what I did yesterday.” You did work yesterday, but can’t remember what.
The coworking manager invites everyone to “morning networking” with croissants. Everyone has to introduce themselves in a circle. You’re not awake yet.
Morning call. The alarm you forgot to turn off starts blaring in the next room. The ringtone is your old school anthem.
The “Who’s in tomorrow?” chat. Everyone answers “we’ll see” and “if it doesn’t rain.” You need to meet three people in person.
9:10. The doorbell: neighbors brought a paint sample and want to discuss the stairwell color. You’re on a call.
The company now tracks attendance by badge swipes. Today’s your “hybrid” day, but it’s pouring and the whole city is gridlocked.
Morning. You’ve been discussing a task the whole call. At the end you realize the selected mic belongs to headphones lying in a drawer.
8:30. The neighbors started laying tiles. Your mic’s noise suppression is turning you into a robot.
Working from the country house. Mom assigns you garden duty: “You’ve got calls, and between them — carrots.” There are a lot of carrots.
Before lunch, a colleague writes: “Did you see my 9 a.m. email?” You did. You just have no idea how to answer it.
You posted an important proposal in the main channel. No replies, but in the next channel twenty people are arguing about pizza.
You’re working from a café; by lunch it’s packed. A woman with a child is looking for a seat, and you’re taking up a table for four.
left: Give up the table and leave

text: You have exactly five minutes between calls. You can hit the bathroom, get water, or answer three messages. Pick one.
You’re sharing your screen when a notification from Mom pops up: “Sweetie, don’t forget your warm socks.” All forty people saw it.
Hybrid day. Colleagues invite you to lunch, but you have a call at 1 p.m. You came to the office just to talk into headphones all day.
right: Take it from an empty room

text: The corporate portal offers a quiz: “Your digital fatigue level.” Result: “Critical.” Send it to the boss?
Kira writes: “Got a minute?” You reply: “Yes.” Her: “Great, then a call in an hour, for an hour and a half.”
The laptop beeps, the phone buzzes, the watch taps your wrist. The same message arrived on three devices. Turn off notifications?
A stranger at the coworking space has been peeking at your screen for ten minutes. On the screen: the secret salary spreadsheet.
Hybrid day. You sit at a free desk, and the keyboard is covered in someone else’s cookie crumbs. The last occupant loved oatmeal cookies.
The desk booking app crashed. A crowd with laptops waits at the entrance to see who grabs the window seat first.
You’ve worked with Saveliy online for a year. Today he came to the office for the first time — he’s a head taller than you imagined. He’s expecting a hug.
After three months remote, the guard doesn’t recognize you and asks for ID. Your ID is at home, next to your morning mug.
Your new noise-canceling headphones are so good you didn’t hear the boss call your name three times in the office.
A London colleague writes at 7 a.m. your time: “Sorry for the early hour!” The message woke you with a duck quack.
New law in the team chat: “Don’t just write ‘Hi’ — ask your question right away.” You just wrote the director “Hi.”
The morning call opens with “How’s everyone feeling?” Twenty squares stay silent, all cameras off.
HR notes you were in the office 1 day out of the required 3 this week. The week ends tomorrow.
Working from the country house. At 8 a.m. the neighbor fires up his lawnmower. You can hear it in the house — and, colleagues say, in the next town.
You tidied up before a call by shoving everything into the closet. A minute later the vacuum falls out — live on air.
You came to work at your favorite café. Twelve people with laptops are already there; the only free seat is a tall bar stool.
The team lead suggests “going over tasks by voice while out walking.” You’re on the move, no screen, and the tasks are an 80-row spreadsheet.
The router is blinking red, stand-up starts in three minutes, and a reboot takes five. Everyone’s waiting for your update.
right: Join by phone from the stairwell

text: The office introduced “team zones.” Your team lives by the elevator, where every minute someone says “oops, wrong floor.”
Lena replied to your long email with “ok.” — with a period. Agreement, offense, or is she just busy?
Your lunch overlaps with a morning meeting for colleagues in another time zone. Eat soup on camera or starve till three?
In the pet-friendly coworking space, someone’s spaniel walks up and rests its head on your lap. No owner in sight, and you’ve got a deadline.
You’re on a call, in a doc, in email and in chat at once. Someone asks: “What do you think?” You have no idea what they’re talking about.
You give a thumbs-up to a colleague’s message about being on sick leave. He replies: “Thanks for being so happy about it.” How to save this?
You asked a question in a thread, the answer came in the main channel. Then a comment in DMs. Then another one by email.
left: Gather it all in one ticket

text: Client demo. You’re sharing your screen, and in the corner a timer glows: “42 minutes until end of day.” The client smirks.
The host split everyone into breakout rooms for 15 minutes. You’re stuck with someone who never unmutes.
The person at the next table asks you to watch his laptop while he pops to the store. You have a call in 20 minutes.
A colleague in Dubai sends a beach photo: “Working from the seaside office.” Outside your window: rain and a soggy pigeon.
You’re editing a shared doc when six more cursors show up. One of them is deleting your paragraph right now.
Mid-call, the host launches a poll: “How interesting is this?” from 1 to 5. Everyone sees the results.
Working from the country house. Grandma has decided the laptop is a TV and asks why such a boring show is on.
Country house, power’s out. The neighbor offers his generator, but it roars like a tractor.
right: Go to the river till evening

text: The team lead writes: “It’s on fire, but no rush.” Five minutes later: “So?” Five more: “Hello??”
The office AC has turned your hybrid day into a polar expedition. Home is warm; here you’ve been issued a blanket and patience.
In the “Remote crew” chat, someone suggests a call to “just work together in silence.” Cameras on. Three hours.
After six hours of screens, your eyes see a cursor where there isn’t one. Two more calls to go.
6 p.m. To “leave work,” you walk out of the apartment, circle the building and come back. A neighbor watches suspiciously.
Your sister asks you to watch her kids “since you’re home anyway.” You have a client call at 6:30 p.m.
Friday, 6 p.m. The coworking space hands out free pizza to members. You’re not a member, just a day guest.
9 p.m. An American colleague asks for a “quick five.” He has morning and energy; you have dinner and a bathrobe.
In the evening you open the doc: 63 comments from colleagues. Half of them say: “What if we did the opposite?”
Evening call. Your only light is the screen, and you look like a horror movie character. Colleagues are already joking.
right: Play along, tell a scary story

text: 7:30 p.m. The workday’s over, but the laptop sits on the dining table, reminding you it exists. Put it away?
At 8 p.m. Grisha sends a 12-minute video explaining a task. Three lines of text would have done it.
Friday evening at the country house. Friends fired up the sauna, and your last report just broke. Signal only on the porch.
The company assigned an online course: “How to work remotely without burning out.” It runs in the evenings, three hours straight.
8:30 p.m. You’re finishing a task at a café when an old classmate walks in: “You still at that same company?”
You accidentally sent the work chat a voice message recorded in your pocket: 40 seconds of rustling and your “oh, whatever.”
Your mother-in-law video-calls to ask why you “do nothing at home all day.” Behind you: the laptop and a mountain of reports.
Before bed you decide to “just glance at email.” There’s one titled “Important, don’t panic.” The panic has already started.
You’ve only talked over video all day. You want to talk to someone in person. Is the store cashier a suitable candidate?
Evening. The chair and the bed share one room. You’ve looked at the bed for eight hours, and it’s been looking back.
After a hybrid day, you sit on the subway and realize the only one you talked to today was the coffee machine. Remote again tomorrow.
8:57. You woke up three minutes before stand-up. Bed to desk is five steps; bed to presentable is an eternity.
Plombir fell asleep in your work backpack. It’s a hybrid day and you need the backpack. Plombir strongly objects.
You need an hour for a call with colleagues across three far-flung time zones. Shared working time: 40 minutes on Tuesday.
Your coffee maker broke. The office is an hour away, the café downstairs five minutes, and the call starts in fifteen.
A new colleague on a call says: “You look nothing like your avatar.” In the avatar you’re twenty-two and at the beach.
Every morning at 9:00 the neighbors’ kid practices the same scale on the violin. Today you’re presenting at 9:15.
The heating hasn’t been turned on yet. You’re working from home in a puffer jacket and a beanie. Camera is mandatory for the morning call.
In the elevator you meet someone you’ve chatted with for a year. You recognize him only by his voice. He doesn’t recognize you.
Nika writes at 8:30: “Are you in the office tomorrow or at home? Trying to decide whether to come.” You haven’t decided yourself.
Morning at the country house. To keep the signal, the laptop has to sit on the windowsill at a 45-degree angle. Stand or sit?
Your office badge photo was taken on a webcam at 7 a.m. Now the guard checks your face against it twice every time.
Morning stand-up, camera on. You put on a shirt, but a colleague points out there’s still a clothespin on your shoulder.
8 a.m. The team lead in the group chat: “If you’re working from home today, react with an emoji.” For some reason nobody wants to go first.
The neighbor’s dog howls every time its owner leaves for work. The owner is hybrid: three days a week of howling.
You’re waiting for a package with your new webcam. The courier writes: “I’ll be there between 9 and 6.” That’s your entire workday of calls.
Sveta turned her camera on at stand-up lying in bed under a duvet. She insists it’s “more productive.” The boss looks at you questioningly.
An email arrives: “Starting Monday — at least three office days a week.” Three months ago you signed a lease on a place way out of town.
You set your status to “Lunch” and went to eat. The boss calls twice: “I saw you’re at lunch, but it’s important.”
You decided to “quickly” make borscht over lunch break. An hour and a half later, the beets are still hard.
You scheduled a meeting forgetting it’s a public holiday for your colleagues abroad. On the call: you and someone’s AI assistant.
The email has one call link, the calendar another, the chat a third. The meeting started a minute ago. Where is everyone?
Auto-captions on the call turn your last name into “Porridge-Bear.” Everyone’s calling you Bear now.
The new camera auto-frames whoever’s talking. Today it took an interest in your cat: the whole call, the cat in close-up.
Brainstorm on the online whiteboard: forty sticky notes, twelve cursors, and someone drawing a cat over the chart.
The coworking meeting room costs $15 an hour. The client is already 20 minutes late; the meter is ticking.
The café cranked up loud dance music. Your client on the call asks: “Are you at a club?”
Your partner decides to vacuum the apartment right in the middle of your presentation. You signal frantically; your partner waves back.
The new manager asks remote staff to send a daily photo of their workspace “for the vibe.” Your workspace is the couch.
Your team uses three messengers. The urgent message landed in the one you open once a week.
You take calls on walks for your health. Phone’s at 3%, and home is fifteen minutes away.
Your night-owl colleague only answers messages after 3 p.m. Your deadline is at 4, and the question is for him.
The eye doctor prescribed a break every 45 minutes. Your calls run 90 minutes nonstop. Ask for a pause?
left: Ask for a break on the call

text: 11 p.m. Vanya writes: “Can you take a look before tomorrow?” No link, no context. A minute later: “You know what I mean.”
New rule: instead of the morning stand-up, a written update by 6 p.m. It’s 6:10, and you just remembered.
The boss recorded a fifteen-minute video address to the team. At the end: “Waiting for your thoughts in the comments by morning.”
Your weekly one-on-one moved to 7 p.m. because the boss is in another time zone. You have movie tickets.
Friday, 6:30 p.m. Team online hangout: everyone sips their own tea and stares at the camera. Only the team lead talks.
The call ended, everyone left, and you’re alone in the room with HR. HR asks: “Since we’re here — how do you like it with us?”
7 p.m. Plombir sits on the keyboard, staring into your soul. His dinner was at 6. Your report isn’t done.
Friday evening. The neighbors are partying, and you have a call with colleagues in Asia at 9 p.m. You can hear the bass through your headphones.
right: Take the call from the bathroom

text: 8 p.m. Your watch reports: “You stood for 4 minutes today.” The rest of the time you sat on calls. Walk around the block?
Sunday, 6 p.m. At the country house, traffic jams on the way out, and Monday is a “hybrid” office day. Leave now or at dawn?
You come back in the evening to seven video messages from colleagues, 3–5 minutes each. Nobody wants to type.
Your freelancer friend invites you to work with her tomorrow from an out-of-town coworking space with a pool. It’s your “hybrid” office day.
You decided to set up an office in the storage closet. By evening you’re standing among mops and jars of jam. The laptop fits; you only partly do.
Mom calls in the evening: “You probably relaxed all day, you’re at home after all.” You had nine calls.
After a day of calls your ears hurt from headphones. In the evening your partner wants to watch a movie — with headphones, so the baby doesn’t wake up.
8:30 p.m. Colleagues in the work chat are discussing a TV show. You missed it while working and now want to chime in.
For the first time all week you didn’t turn your camera on. The boss writes: “Everything okay? We haven’t seen you for five calls now.”
right: Promise to turn it on tomorrow

text: The café you worked from all day is closing. The barista gives you a free croissant as their “staff member of the month.”
The company launched a virtual office: your little avatar has to “walk” to the meeting room. You’re stuck inside a pixel ficus.
Country house. To catch a signal, the neighbor hung the modem on a birch tree. The wind sways the birch, and your stand-up sways with it.
You’re tethering from your phone. Your carrier texts: “300 MB left.” A video call starts in five minutes.
Hybrid day. On the subway you notice you left home in your house slippers. Two stops to the office, four back home.
First office day in a month. In the kitchen: expired cookies and milk that has become cheese. Breakfast?
Your coworking pass expired yesterday. The admin offers a “guest” day at full price, with a bonus: tea.
It’s 10 a.m. for you, but your colleague nine time zones ahead has already had lunch and sent you seven messages. The last: “Hello, are you there?”
Kirill recommends a “mouse jiggler” so your status always shows “online.” He says half the department has one.
You blocked “focus time” from 10 to 12. Colleagues booked three meetings over it without looking.
Hybrid office day. Everyone’s calling from phone booths, and the line is like a clinic waiting room. Your call starts in 2 minutes.
It’s “Bring Your Pet Day.” A colleague brought a parrot that screams “Turn your camera on!” every ten minutes.
You came to the office for some human contact, but the whole team is home today. You’re in an empty meeting room on a call with them.
You need to sign a paper contract. No printer at home, the office is an hour away, and the client’s courier arrives at 1 p.m.
A colleague writes: “You in the office today? Bring my mug to my place, it’s on the windowsill.” Her place is across town.
You work by the window. The whole courtyard can see you’ve sat in the same pose since 8 a.m. The old ladies on the bench are waving at you.
Your hybrid desk-mate believes that since he booked the desk first, the drawer is his too. Your tea stash is in that drawer.
Mid-call, a wasp flies in from the porch and lands on you, then on the screen, then on you. Colleagues can see the panic.
Working from the country house. The hammock in the apple tree’s shade beckons. The laptop has battery, but the signal there is “one bar.”
You’re conducting an online interview. The candidate is clearly reading answers off the screen — eyes darting left to right.
Hybrid meeting. The meeting room mic picks up a colleague’s chip-crunching loudest of all. Remote attendees hear only crunching.
The client asks: “On the call, pretend you’re in the office — this is a serious project.” You’re in the kitchen, fridge magnets behind you.
You asked a question in chat three days ago. Today the reply arrives: “Is this still relevant?” Not anymore — you did it yourself.
The team votes in chat on when to move stand-up. It’s a tie, and yours is the deciding vote.
You started the washing machine during a long meeting. The meeting’s over, but you have four more: the laundry waits till evening.
You’re at a café and urgently need the restroom. The laptop with open work documents is on the table.
left: Ask your neighbor to watch it

text: HR introduces an “online coffee break” at 3 p.m.: everyone drinks coffee on camera and shares news. You’ve just hit your flow.
Your browser weighs more than you do. 63 tabs, and somewhere in one of them music is playing. Find it or close everything?
You hit “Leave,” but the screen froze. You’re live for ten more seconds with a “finally, silence” face.
You work on a timer: 25 minutes on, 5 off. A colleague demands a call right in the middle of your fifth pomodoro.
You’re working on the balcony when the lady on the next balcony starts telling you about her seedlings. You’re in headphones, but she’s sure you can hear.
The HR chatbot asks: “How do you feel working remotely?” Options: “Great,” “Good,” “Fine.” Nothing else.
Before a big presentation you do a test call with yourself. Echo, feedback whistle, two of your faces. Something went wrong.
They’ve started repairing the road under your window. A jackhammer now features in every call you take.
A colleague bought a second camera and now shows himself from above, then from the side, “for dynamics.” You’re getting seasick.
7 p.m. A colleague in Bali is just starting the day and cheerfully writes: “Let’s discuss everything!” You have dinner and dreams of sleep.
Sunday evening. Tomorrow’s an office day, and you need to remember where your badge, headphones and non-saggy pants are.
right: Figure it out in the morning

text: A therapist recommends an “end-of-day ritual”: close the laptop and say “I’m done.” You say it to an empty room. The cat stares.
Your partner declares the desk their territory in the evenings. Your laptop has been on that desk since 8 a.m. and isn’t leaving.
At night you dream your mic is on during an all-hands call. You wake up and check the laptop. It’s off.
You found a second monitor online at half price. The seller lives out of town and will wait until 9 p.m.
6:30 p.m. The coworking space is hosting a mixer for members. You need to finish a text, and everyone around is mingling.
Night at the country house, a sky full of stars. Laptop open on the porch: one report left. The screen glow has attracted every moth around.
Timur was “online” all day with a green dot. In the evening he admits a mouse jiggler kept the dot green while he went fishing. He asks you to keep quiet.
You finished the last call and realized you didn’t open a window all day. The apartment is as stuffy as a server room.
In the evening you write a daily recap in chat for colleagues in other time zones. The essay stretches to a full page.
Evening call from the bathroom because the kids are asleep in the room. The acoustics make you sound like an opera singer.
After an office day it feels like you’ve forgotten how to talk to people in person. You told the cashier “You’re on mute” three times.
right: Sign up for a social skills course

text: Before bed, the calendar reminds you: “9 meetings tomorrow.” The last one: “How to reduce the number of meetings.”
A former colleague writes: “We’re fully remote and no calls before noon. Want to join us?” You look at your 9 meetings.
Friday, 6 p.m. Colleagues are saying goodbye in chat: everyone writes “Have a great weekend!” Forty messages so far, sound on.
6:40 a.m., security check. The officer asks you to turn on your work laptop, but you changed the password last night and can’t remember it. The line behind you sighs. What now?
Check-in: your suitcase of client samples weighs 27 kg instead of 23. The excess fee equals three days of your per diem. Pay?
A colleague with a lounge card gets you into the business lounge. There are free pancakes, and your report isn’t finished. Pancakes or work?
A text from the airline: “Upgrade to business class for $100.” Accounting will never reimburse that. Splurge?
Flight to a business trip. The guy in the window seat has spent two hours pitching his startup and wants your number “for investment.” How to escape?
right: Take his card for the boss

text: At 7:20 a.m. the boss writes: “Since you’re at the airport, buy a gift for the partners at duty-free. Receipt later.” No budget, and “later” is a stretchy concept. Buy it?
Reception: “Your room won’t be ready until 2 p.m.” You’re off a night train, the meeting is at 10, and you need a shower now. What now?
right: Go to the meeting as is

text: Business trip. One last pancake at the buffet — and the host company’s director is reaching for it too. Let him have it?
Business trip, 8:15 a.m. The hotel iron left a brown mark on your shirt, perfectly iron-shaped. Meeting in an hour. Your move?
left: Button the jacket all the way
right: Run out for a new shirt

text: A trip six time zones away. It’s 9 a.m. local, 3 a.m. for you, and your body insists it’s the dead of night. Survive the morning meeting?
The airport taxi driver swears he knows a “shortcut through the cottages.” The GPS disagrees, and the meeting is in forty minutes. Trust him?
You and a colleague are going on a business trip. In the morning he admits he left his passport at home, and the train leaves in half an hour. What do you do?
The hosts meet you at the station with a sign with your name misspelled in giant letters. Next to them, a photographer for their company news. Smile?
Your per diem hits your card today, the day the trip starts. People are waiting, but room-service breakfast costs half a day’s allowance. Order it?
The travel agency booked you a hotel “in the center.” The center turned out to be the center of the next village, an hour by bus from the client’s office. What now?
Business trip, 7:30 a.m. Your key wristband won’t open the door, and you’re standing in the hallway in a towel after the pool. The client’s delegation walks by. What now?
left: Run to reception in a towel

text: Your first business trip abroad. A colleague advises packing an immersion heater, five packs of instant noodles and an extension cord. Take them?
Business trip. The hosts invite you on a factory tour: six workshops, a hard hat, two hours on foot. The report for your boss is burning. Go?
Accounting calls you mid-trip: “Why are there two coffees on your receipt? There’s only one of you.” Explain the second was for a partner?
In the trip chat, colleagues are deciding where to eat on per diem: the factory canteen or a restaurant “on our own dime.” You have the deciding vote. Where?
On a business trip, a partner insists you try the signature local dish — something cold and wobbly. He’s watching you closely. Eat it?
Housekeeping mixed up the rooms, and your laptop ended up in the room of an unknown delegation. They’re in meetings till evening. Wait or hunt?
The client meeting is running long, and you’re about to miss your train home. The client has just gotten to the main point. Leave or stay?
Last day of the trip. The department expects souvenirs, and you have one hour and a single station shop with magnets and gingerbread. How much to buy?
Accounting: “Per diem is counted by departure dates. You left at 11:58 p.m., so that day doesn’t count.” Fight over two minutes?
A call from your hotel room. The only spot with internet is by the bed, and behind you is a wall-sized rug with deer on it. Camera on?
left: On — the deer are a vibe

text: Business trip. You absentmindedly ate the minibar nuts. Price tag: $8. Your per diem won’t cover that. Now what?
left: Buy the same, swap them in

text: Business trip. The host company’s director decided to personally show you every monument in town. Your client meeting is in three hours. What now?
You’re visiting a branch, and the local staff complain to you about head office as if you represent it. There are many of them, and they’re upset. Your reaction?
A local accountant asks you to take a document folder, a jar of jam and a cat in a carrier back to head office. The cat is “for the chief accountant, she knows.” Take it?
You’re offered a two-day extension of your trip “since you’re there anyway.” At home: your cat and an unread inbox. Agree?
Your train is delayed three hours. The station has a waiting room with outlets and a café with pastries. Work or rest?
Colleagues in chat ask: “Since you’re on a trip, fill out our reports — you’ve got a quiet hotel room.” Four reports. Agree?
Sleeper compartment on a business trip. Your fellow travelers lay out chicken, eggs and pickles and insist on sharing. You have a laptop and a call in ten minutes. Your move?
right: Go to the vestibule with the laptop

text: The trip report needs a photo “in the middle of negotiations.” The talks were yesterday, and nobody took a picture. What will you come up with?
Business trip, 11 p.m. There’s a bar outside your window, playing the same song until 2 a.m. You forgot your earplugs, of course. What now?
left: Go to the bar — no sleep anyway
right: Ask reception for a new room

text: Business trip, 7 p.m. The partners invite you to the sauna “to strengthen relations.” You don’t like saunas or partners in bedsheets. Go?
Business trip. Evening in the room: the TV only shows a fishing channel, and the Wi-Fi password is “at the front desk.” How will you spend the evening?
Business trip. The hotel has a gym, free until 10 p.m. You meant to “finally take care of yourself.” It’s 9:15. Go?
Business trip. A colleague invites you to “see the city” tonight, but his eyes say the city is the karaoke bar next to the hotel. Go?
9:30 p.m. Boarding the flight home. A woman asks to swap seats so she can sit with her husband. Her seat: middle row, middle seat, by the toilet. Agree?
The trip’s over, and your per diem is barely touched. Accounting isn’t asking about the rest. Treat yourself to dinner with the change?
Evening at the airport, back from the trip. The boss writes: “Since you’re in town, swing by the office, let’s discuss results.” It’s 9 p.m. Go?
Business trip. Reception offers late checkout for half your daily allowance; otherwise you leave at noon, and your train is at 10 p.m. Pay?
right: Sit in the lobby with bags

text: You landed, but your suitcase came out on the belt wide open, with your bunny pajamas on top. A colleague from sales is standing right there. Your reaction?
The “Kazan trip” chat was never deleted after you got back. Colleagues keep posting memes, and you’ve been made admin. What now?
Friday evening. Accounting reminds you they need a paper boarding pass for the return flight. It’s still on the plane, in the seat pocket. What now?
You’re back from a three-day trip. The cat sits pointedly with its back to you, and the neighbor who fed it awaits a report. Your plan?
Mom calls while you’re on the trip: “Are you dressing warmly? Send me a photo of you in a hat.” You didn’t bring a hat. Your answer?
left: Snap a photo in a hood

text: Business trip. Your roommate suggests “saving the per diem” by eating only from the supermarket next to the hotel all week. Agree?
9:10 a.m. The conference organizer hands you a slide clicker. It only goes backward, and there’s no spare. Your talk is in twenty minutes. Your plan?
Before your talk, the sound engineer clips on a lavalier mic and warns: “It’s always on, even in the restroom.” You nod. The talk is in an hour. What next?
left: Take it off during the break

text: Conference morning. At registration everyone gets a tote bag of swag: notebook, pen, socks and a bottle-opener keychain. The socks are size XS. What do you do?
right: Wear them for luck on stage

text: The moderator asks you to cut your self-introduction to one sentence. You spent a week on it and even mentioned a school math contest. Cut it?
left: Cut it to your job title

text: 9 a.m. The colleague speaking before you confesses: “My talk ends with your conclusions — I peeked.” Your reaction?
Conference at a hotel. In the morning you discover speakers eat in a separate room with pancakes, while attendees get dry cookies. You’re a speaker; your colleagues aren’t. Where do you go?
Your morning talk is being streamed online. The first comment in the stream chat: “Did the speaker raid grandma’s closet for that jacket?” How do you react?
A conference with international guests. Before the start, the interpreter asks for your script, but you planned to improvise. Half an hour to go. What do you do?
The organizers mixed up the program, and your talk “Optimizing Warehouse Accounting” is in the “Art & Inspiration” track. Present anyway?
The boss writes before the conference: “Be sure to mention our new product, but without it sounding like an ad.” The product is accounting software. What now?
Conference morning. The registration line is forty minutes long, and there’s no separate speaker desk. Your talk is first. Cut the line?
9:30. You open your deck on the organizers’ computer, and every font has turned into little squares. Talk in five minutes. What do you do?
After your talk, the first person to raise a hand begins “not so much a question as a comment” — for ten minutes. The timer is ticking. Interrupt?
From the audience: “Why is your product worse than your competitors’?” Judging by the badge, he’s a manager at a competitor. Your answer?
In the middle of your talk, the lights go out. Only the emergency exit sign and your phone are glowing. The audience waits. Keep going?
Coffee break. At the pastry table you realize the speaker next to you is the one whose talk you loudly called “fluff” this morning. He recognized you. What do you do?
At a workshop the host picks a volunteer to demonstrate the “trust fall.” He’s looking straight at you. Agree?
The event photographer asks speakers for an “inspired shot” by the banner: gazing into the distance, pointing toward the future. Pose?
Conference lunch. An industry celebrity sits down at your table and eats in silence. You’ve long dreamed of meeting him. Strike up a conversation?
A colleague came to support your talk and sat in the front row. Three minutes in, he fell asleep and is softly snoring. Visible from the stage. Your move?
You’re presenting at an online conference from a meeting room. Behind the glass wall, the cleaner starts mopping and waves at the camera. What now?
right: Turn the laptop to the wall

text: After your talk, a trade journalist asks for “a few words for the press” and turns on a recorder. PR never approved this. Talk?
You’re on the jury of a startup contest. The third project in a row is an “AI for matching socks.” The founder looks at you hopefully. Your score?
You step on stage and realize your printed notes are on the coffee-break table — across the entire hall. What do you do?
The previous speaker ran fifteen minutes over, and the moderator asks you to “keep it to five.” You had twenty. Squeeze it?
The organizers announce a “networking game”: collect five strangers’ signatures in ten minutes. Prize: a thermos. Play?
A sponsor booth hands out free coffee, but only if you fill out a twenty-question survey. You really need coffee. Fill it out?
The boss is watching your livestream and DMs you every two minutes: “Louder,” “Don’t slouch,” “Smile.” Your phone buzzes on the podium. What do you do?
The organizers sent your talk ratings: average 4.8, and one comment: “Boring, but nice outfit.” Forward the report to the boss?
The afterparty. The host hands every speaker maracas and announces a “jam session.” You’re the last one who hasn’t played. Your move?
right: Slip off to the coat check

text: Evening after the conference. Organizers ask speakers to sign consent to use the recording “in all media, forever.” Sign?
7:30 p.m. An email: “Your talk was voted best — please repeat it at the plenary session tomorrow at 9:00.” You’re already on the train home. What do you do?
A colleague who stayed at the office asks you to present “the most useful bits of the conference” to the whole department tonight. There were two useful slides. What now?
Evening train back from the conference. Your neighbor in the car is the very man you argued with at the session. He suggests “finishing the debate” over tea. Agree?
Offsite strategy session, 9 a.m. The facilitator hands out sticky notes in three colors and asks you to “express your feelings about the company through color.” Which one?
Strategy session at a country retreat. Wake-up at 7 a.m. for “energizing exercises with the CEO.” You see him in leggings. Go?
Strategy session. The facilitator asks everyone to name “the company’s main enemy.” Silence; the CEO smiles. You’re first in line. What will you say?
Offsite. At the retreat you share a bunk bed with the CFO. He offers you the top bunk, “young people’s privilege.” Your reply?
Strategy session. For “full immersion,” everyone’s phones went into a box until evening, and a courier with documents is about to call you. What do you do?
At the strategy session you’re assigned the “Threats” section of a SWOT analysis. All that comes to mind is “the next strategy session.” What do you write?
At the strategy session the CEO asks: “If you were the director, what would you change first?” The room freezes. Answer honestly?
Offsite. After four hours debating the mission statement, two options remain: “We Do Better” and “We Do Good.” Vote. Your pick?
The facilitator announces an exercise: walk around and give compliments. You must praise the manager who sank your project yesterday. Your compliment?
At the offsite, catering brought lunch for thirty, but fifty people came. You’re at the serving table. Split it evenly?
left: Give it all away, go hungry

text: Three hours into the strategy session the CEO announces: “Conclusion: we carry on as before, but with enthusiasm.” A colleague whispers: “We drove two hours for this?” Respond?
Evening at the offsite. On the program: “informal campfire with songs about company values.” The mosquitoes have already gathered. Go?
Evening at the offsite. The CEO suggests “continuing the brainstorm in the sauna.” Your brain has been stormed since 9 a.m. Go?
7 p.m., last day of the offsite. You’re told to turn eight flipchart sheets of scribbles into a final document by morning. What will you do?
The session’s over, and on a flipchart you find a colleague’s drawing: the CEO as a dragon. The room is about to be cleared with management present. What do you do?
left: Tear it off as a keepsake

text: 9 a.m., the internal hackathon kicks off. Teams form in five minutes, and two are fighting over you: “AI for Lunches” and “A Bot That Scolds Deadlines.” Which one?
Morning of hackathon day two. You woke up on a beanbag in a meeting room with a keyboard print on your cheek. A teammate is already writing: “Everything’s broken.” Your move?
Hackathon. The organizers are handing out energy drinks by the case. Your left eye is already twitching, and there are ten more hours of coding ahead. Take some?
At 8 a.m. your hackathon captain decides to “pivot”: instead of a vacation bot, we’re building an app for walking office plants. Your reaction?
Hackathon, 10 a.m. Turns out your team has five people and all are analysts. Nobody can code, but the spreadsheets are ready. What do you do?
right: Learn to code on the fly

text: Hackathon. A guy from another team at your table suggests “swapping ideas.” His eyes are shifty, and your laptop is open. Agree?
Hackathon demo. Three minutes in, your app crashes and the screen shows in huge letters: “error: everything is bad.” The jury is watching. Your move?
Hackathon. Pizza came for everyone, but your team got stuck on a bug, and all that’s left are crusts with pineapple. What now?
You drew the short straw to pitch the team project. Three minutes, thirty cat pictures on the slides, and not a single number. Present?
The boss drops by the hackathon “just to watch” and sits next to you. Ten minutes later he’s telling you which buttons to press. Your move?
Hackathon results are in. Your team took second place. The prize: your idea gets implemented. First place got a day off. Celebrate?
The hackathon’s over, and the CEO suddenly loves your idea. Now it “needs to launch within a month, by its author, alongside the day job.” Take it on?
Hackathon, 11 p.m. The organizers turned off the lights so “everyone gets two hours of sleep.” Your team wants to code by phone light. You in?
right: Sleep on a mat in the corner

text: Hackathon, midnight. Someone put on music to keep people awake. It’s a military march. Half the room is marching in circles. Join them?
The hackathon ended at 7 p.m. You’ve slept four hours in two days, and colleagues want to “celebrate the demo” at a bar. Your call?
Hackathon. Your team coded late into the night, and a teammate quietly committed everything to someone else’s repo. Demo’s in the morning. Your move?
Open house for students. You’re stationed at the entrance with a sign: “Ask me a question!” It’s 9 a.m., here comes the first group. Smile?
Open house morning. HR asks you to clear your desk of anything “informal”: the cat mug, photos, the pack of cookies. Working without cookies is sad. Clear it?
right: Hide the cookies under the desk

text: Open house. In front of your boss, a student asks: “Do you really work till six, or is that just what the website says?” Your answer?
First-graders are visiting for the open house. One of them sat in your chair, pressed every key and asks: “Are you the boss here?” Answer?
Open house. HR asks you to stage a “live work meeting” for guests in a meeting room. Script: everyone smiles and takes notes. Play along?
Open house guests ask to see “the most interesting thing in the office.” On your floor, that’s the talking coffee machine. Show them?
left: Put on a coffee machine show

text: “Take Your Kids to Work Day.” A colleague’s child decided to help with your report and has already typed half a page of “kggggggg.” The report is due at 3. What do you do?
Kids at work day. The boss’s six-year-old son asks you: “Does Dad yell at work too, like at home?” Everyone nearby goes quiet. Your answer?
Evening after the open house. A student sent you a résumé and an internship request, signed “you were the most fun.” Pass it to HR?
8 a.m., company blood drive. You donate on an empty stomach, and donors get the day off. An urgent task awaits you at the office. Go donate?
Company volunteer trip to a dog shelter. You showed up in white sneakers, and the job is walking six dogs through mud. What do you do?
The department joined a charity paper drive. In the morning you notice someone put your working drafts in the collection box. What do you do?
right: Let it go — it’s for a good cause

text: HR announces a “Give a thing, warm a heart” drive. In the donation box there’s a sweater you recognize: you gave it to a colleague for New Year’s. Your reaction?
Charity auction at the office. The lot: “lunch with the CEO.” Bids are climbing, and colleagues nudge you: “You wanted that promotion!” Bid?
The office collects bottle caps for a good cause. One colleague pointedly pours everyone water and stashes all the caps in his own desk. What do you do?
Volunteer event: planting trees by the business center. You get a shovel, a sapling and instructions. The ground is frozen, colleagues are filming. Your move?
Charity bake sale. You bought your own pie, baked that morning — nobody else was buying it. Colleagues noticed. Your reaction?
The CEO proposes donating a day’s earnings of the department to charity. Open vote; your boss votes first: “Yes.” Your vote?
Charity run: every kilometer an employee runs becomes a donation. You’ve run two, and a colleague insists you can “just ride a scooter.” What now?
Volunteer trip to a retirement home. A grandma in a wheelchair demands a game of checkers “for stakes.” The bus leaves in an hour. Play?
Staff charity concert night. The host announces you: “And now, for the fund, singing for us...” You never agreed to this. The mic is already in your hand. Sing?
right: Give a speech about the fund

text: 7 p.m. The team chat: “Shelter food drive — who can drive the bags over tonight?” Twelve bags; you have a car. Take them?
After work, the office is collecting toys for a children’s hospital. You promised to bring “lots,” but at home you only found a plush cactus and a Rubik’s cube. What now?
left: Buy new ones on the way

text: Evening. An email: a charity thanks you “for your generous donation.” Colleagues pledged it in your name, but you still have to hand over the money. How do you react?
right: Find out whose idea it was

text: 7:30 a.m., the company run starts. You got bib number 1 — because the CEO is running as number 2 and “wants to overtake someone important.” How do you run?
Race morning. Team T-shirts were printed with “Faster than the deadline!” but they’re all size XS. Yours is tighter than a mortgage. Wear it?
HR hired a corporate trainer, and at 8 a.m. he’s running a plank challenge in the open-plan office. Whoever lasts longest wins “an hour with no calls.” Join in?
It’s “Bike to Work Day.” You don’t own a bike, and colleagues are already joking about “the guest from the subway.” Your decision?
Inter-office sports day. You’re signed up for tug-of-war with the heaviest guy from accounting. He suggests the “dead anchor tactic.” Listen to him?
left: Lie down as an anchor too

text: The captain of the office volleyball team writes at 7:40 a.m.: “Final today, we’re short, come even as a sub.” You haven’t played since school. Go?
The company step tracker shows you walked the least in the whole company this week. The leaderboard is on the portal’s homepage. What will you do?
9 a.m., “office yoga.” The instructor asks you to lie on a mat right in the meeting room and “let go of work thoughts.” The boss watches through the glass. Let go?
Five-a-side final: your department vs. sales. You’re in goal, and the penalty taker is the head of sales — your future approver. Save it?
Lunchtime company chess tournament. Your opponent is the CEO, and he’s clearly blundered his queen. Colleagues freeze by the board. Take the queen?
Inter-department relay. Your leg: the egg-and-spoon race. The egg is raw, and you’re in work pants. The marketing runner is already off. How do you run?
Office darts tournament. The board hangs on the CFO’s office door, and he’s about to walk out for a meeting right now. Throw?
Company 30 km bike ride. At kilometer 15 you spot a pancake café, and there’s nobody behind you. Rest or keep pedaling?
Finish line of the company run. The photographer asks you to show “the joy of victory.” You came 43rd out of 45. Pose?
In the department sports chat, everyone posts their workouts. You haven’t posted anything since Monday, and people are “affectionately” tagging you. Your reply?
Mid-meeting, the boss challenges the department: whoever does the most squats today gets Friday remote. You’re sitting right next to him. In?
The break room got a table hockey game. Finance hogs it every lunch and won’t let “rookies” play. Today’s your chance. Challenge them?
Team-building at a climbing gym. You’re halfway up, fingers shaking, and from below: “Go, the department flag is at the top!” Six meters to go. Climb?
Company yoga. The instructor asks you to close your eyes and imagine you’re a tree. You imagined a tree on vacation. Someone nearby is snoring. Your move?
Company field day. You got the sack race; your partner got a bucket of water to carry on his head. Swap?
You biked to work for the fitness leaderboard. The bike rack is full of colleagues’ scooters. Lock it to the fence by the entrance?
right: Haul the bike to your desk

text: Sports day. In archery you accidentally hit the neighboring team’s target and scored them a ten. They’re cheering. Tell the referee?
6:30 p.m. The company running club starts from the office. You’re in work shoes; your sneakers are at home. Colleagues are waiting outside. Run?
Evening match between departments. Your boss is up front and has missed an open goal for the third time. He’s looking at you for a pass. Pass again?
Evening. Bowling tournament final, and your last roll decides who gets the cup. You’ve rolled three gutter balls in a row. Your move?
right: Give the roll to the best player

text: Company basketball. The opponents are the lawyers; they argue with the ref after every shot and have already demanded the official record. Hour three. Your move?
Evening, company gym in the basement. Your boss is on the next treadmill and clearly speeding up to beat you. Accept the challenge?
Your team won the company’s rotating trophy. The captain is going on vacation and asks you to keep the cup at your place “until the next tournament.” Take it?
right: Leave it in a meeting room

text: Company ski trip. Your first time on downhill skis, and colleagues invite you to “the red run, the view is amazing.” The sun is setting. Your choice?
Morning. HR sends a reminder: “You’re signed up for the talent show with the act ‘Juggling.’” You didn’t sign up and you don’t juggle. What do you do?
You’ve been asked to host the talent show. The script arrived at 8 a.m.: “Jokes along the way — at host’s discretion.” There are no jokes and no discretion. Prepare?
A colleague is preparing a talent show act and warms up her voice every morning in the meeting room next to your desk. Today: scales for half an hour. Your move?
Talent show. Your department is doing a “human pyramid.” As the lightest one, you’re assigned the very top. Rehearsal at 9 a.m. Agree?
You’re on the talent show jury. Your own boss is reciting his own poetry. Rhymes include “deadline — headline.” Your score?
At rehearsal, the sound guy played your act to the wrong track: heavy metal instead of a romantic ballad. It sounds surprisingly good. Keep it?
Talent show. An accountant performs a magic trick: asks you to draw a card and “think of your bonus amount.” The card is the two of spades. The room roars. Your reaction?
Your talent act is blind speed-typing. On stage you discover the keyboard has a foreign layout. The audience waits. Your move?
Your department is staging a skit for the talent show, and you’re writing the script. Everyone wants the lead, and one colleague just wants “to stand there looking pretty.” How do you cast it?
The CEO suddenly decides to perform at the talent show and picks you as his dance partner. No rehearsal; the music is a tango. Agree?
Talent show. Your act is a parody of management. At the dress rehearsal, management itself walks in and sits in the front row. Perform it?
Office talent show: the audience award is decided by a chat vote. A teammate writes: “You vote for me, I vote for you.” Deal?
Talent show. Right before you, a colleague performed your exact act: poems by the same poet. The applause hasn’t died down. What do you do?
Talent show finale. You won, and the grand prize is hosting the next show and writing its script. Your reaction?
Talent show night. Your act isn’t in the program — the organizer “forgot.” You spent three weeks learning tap dance. Go on unannounced?
After the talent show, a video of your virtuoso whistling went viral across the company. Tonight the CEO asks you to repeat it at an investor meeting. Your move?
The talent show’s over, and nobody can take the props — a two-meter cardboard dragon. The organizer is eyeing your car. Take it?
Talent show. Right before you, a colleague’s three-year-old sang a song about a hedgehog and got a standing ovation. Go on after that?
After the talent show, you’re asked to “urgently set up a fan club” for the winner — your boss. He doesn’t object. Create the chat?
Pancake Week at the office. HR announced a “Department Pancake” contest: every team brings a stack of pancakes by 10 a.m. Your team has no pan and no plan. What do you do?
right: Buy them, pass off as homemade

text: April 1, 9 a.m. A note on your monitor: “Report to the CEO immediately.” The handwriting looks suspiciously like your neighbor’s. Go?
right: Stick it on the neighbor’s monitor

text: April 1. Colleagues taped over your mouse sensor and flipped your keyboard upside down. Client call in ten minutes. How will you get revenge?
Morning of the company’s birthday. Everyone is asked to wear brand colors — orange and turquoise. Your closet holds only gray. What now?
The company’s birthday. At the entrance everyone gets party hats and noisemakers, and at 9:30 you have serious talks with a bank. Wear the hat?
right: Stash the noisemaker in your bag

text: Secret Santa draw. You got the CEO, and the gift budget is $10. He’s already hinted he likes good coffee. What do you give?
Morning. A Secret Santa gift on your desk: a weight-loss kit and a book called “How to Stop Being Late.” Colleagues await your reaction. Your move?
The last morning before the holidays. The office manager asks everyone to remove tinsel from their desks by 11 a.m., or face a “Christmas tree fine.” Clean up?
The CEO is recording a New Year’s video address and needs five people in the background “showing joy at the year’s results.” You were walking by. Join?
HR announced “Pajama Friday.” You came in pajamas, but it was moved to next week — the email went out last night. What now?
It’s Accountants’ Day. The department chipped in for a cake for accounting, but someone has to carry it across the office. You’re the closest. Carry it?
Programmers’ Day. The IT team expects congratulations, and your department forgot. Their stand-up is in half an hour. What can you pull off?
Company Family Day: you can bring the kids to the office. At 9:15 your child has already found the fire alarm button and is looking at you. Your move?
Morning of the company picnic. You’re in charge of the grill. The coals won’t catch, and management is already standing there with plates. Your plan?
left: Fan it with a report folder
right: Hand the grill to an enthusiast

text: Halloween. The office manager hands out pumpkins for a carving contest, and yours weighs eight kilos. A blunt knife is included. Carve?
right: Draw a face with a marker

text: Company health day: at 9 a.m. a nurse checks blood pressure for free. The whole office is in line, work has stopped. Join the line?
Today is your profession’s official holiday. Nobody in management has congratulated you, and it’s already 11:30. Remind the boss?
The office manager wants a “childhood photo” by 10 a.m. for a “Guess the Colleague” board. In your only photo you’re crying in a bunny costume. Bring it?
right: Bring a photo of your cat

text: December 31, 9 a.m. You’re almost alone in the office, and an email arrives: “urgent, before year end.” Year end is in fifteen hours. Your move?
The morning after the announcement: the office party will be on a riverboat. You get seasick even in elevators. The boss says you “absolutely must be there.” Your reply?
The company bought three crates of tangerines for the holidays. They’re parked by your desk, and the whole office keeps walking past you “for vitamins.” Your move?
left: Hand them out with a smile

text: The company’s birthday. The CEO asks people to share “their brightest moment at the company,” live in front of the whole office. You’re next. What will you tell?
April 1. A colleague posted in the group chat: “Everyone gets a short day today.” Half the office is already in the elevator. You know it’s a prank. Tell them?
You forgot to buy your Secret Santa gift. The swap is at 11 a.m. In your desk drawer: an unopened planner and last year’s greeting card. How to save yourself?
The morning after the office party. Someone’s high-heeled shoe is on your desk, and the team chat asks: “Has anyone seen my shoe and my reputation?” What do you do?
right: Post a photo of the find

text: Morning. The company photographer sent everyone the party photos. In every single shot of you, your mouth is full. They’re already on the portal. Your reaction?
Before the holidays you’re asked to hand-sign a hundred client cards by 11 a.m. The pen skips every other stroke, and your hand already hurts. Your move?
Office party on a riverboat. An hour in, it turns out you can’t dock until 11 p.m. The seasickness is coming. How do you survive?
Office party. The host announces joke awards, and you get “Chief Latecomer.” The certificate is already framed, and the room expects a speech. Your speech?
Office party at a museum. The guide asks people not to touch the exhibits, and a colleague is already taking selfies in a knight’s helmet. Security is heading over. Your move?
The party’s over. You lost your coat-check ticket, and the attendant demands “a description of the jacket with distinguishing features.” Everyone’s jacket is black. Your move?
left: Describe it down to the button

text: Out-of-town office party, 11:30 p.m. The bus is dropping everyone home, and your address is last on the route. Two and a half hours of riding. What do you do?
right: Split a taxi with a colleague

text: Office party with a live band. The lead singer heard you’re “employee of the year” and calls you up for a duet. You’ve never heard the song. Go up?
Sushi workshop at the office party. Your roll fell apart; the CEO’s turned out fine. He offers you his “for motivation.” Your move?
Theme party: “Jobs of the Future.” Everyone came as astronauts, and you came as a “remote work specialist” — in pajamas, with a laptop. How do you hold up?
Office party. The host runs a contest: “Who can fastest find a work photo on their phone?” Your gallery is full of memes about the boss. Take part?
Office party. The boss takes the mic and starts a toast “about every employee.” There are twenty of you; he’s on number four. The main course is getting cold. Your move?
At 10 p.m. the paid time at the venue ends. The manager says any extension is on the guests. Colleagues look at you as the organizer. Pay?
Company picnic. A downpour starts, and there’s one tent for all of accounting plus the CEO. Space is tight. Let him in?
Family day is wrapping up. Your kid befriended the CEO’s kid and refuses to leave. The CEO suggests “playing for another hour.” Stay?
Holiday party raffle: you won the grand prize — a goose. A live one. From a client’s farm. What do you do?
Secret Santa night. Your gift — pricey and beautiful — went to the person who gave you a paper snowflake. Your reaction?
Halloween at the office. You stayed late, and colleagues dressed as zombies are preparing a “surprise” behind the door. You see it in your monitor’s reflection. What do you do?
Halloween party. You came as a bedsheet ghost — and so did the CEO. People keep mixing you up. Now his wife is walking toward you. Your move?
Pancake Week at the office. Tonight in the courtyard they’re burning an effigy of “The Annual Report.” The effigy came from your department — and so did the papers inside it. Your move?
The company’s birthday. In the lobby there’s a logo-shaped cake, and the CEO asks you to cut it “for everyone.” Two hundred staff, a cake for fifty. Cut it?
right: Hand the knife to the CEO

text: The evening before the holidays. The office is decorated, but the CEO is holding “the last wrap-up meeting of the year” at 7 p.m. Champagne is already on the tables. Your move?
Evening after the party. The videographer sent a 40-minute clip in which you’re on screen for 38. HR wants to show it at the all-hands. What do you do?
Office party. The boss approaches with a glass: “Let’s drop the formalities — tell me what you really think of me.” Everyone nearby goes quiet. Your answer?
Company karaoke’s over, and the scoreboard ranked your duet with a colleague “the best.” Now the team chat calls you “the star couple.” How to react?
Office party at a country club. Turns out there’s a skating rink on site, and all you brought are patent leather shoes. Colleagues are already on the ice. Join them?
Office party. The dance contest goes to the pair that lasts longest. Your partner is the CFO, who apparently has decided never to give up. Your move?
11:40 p.m. The party’s nearly over. The waiters offer to pack up leftovers, and colleagues are already filling containers. You too?
At the office party the host jokes about your department: “And here are the folks who keep breaking everything.” The CEO laughs loudly. Your response?
Team party for closing the quarter. Pizza for twelve, but eight more people from the next department dropped by “to say hi.” What do you do?
Office party. The draw sat you at management’s table. They’re serving bony fish, and everyone watches you wrestle it with a fork. Your move?
Office party at an escape room. Your team is locked in the “bunker,” and the only key is with a colleague who went to the restroom an hour ago. What do you do?
The company’s birthday evening. The CEO announces: “Everyone will leave a wish in a time capsule — we’ll open it in ten years.” What do you write?
You’re assigned to buy holiday gifts for thirty people. The store closes at 8 p.m., and there are fifteen fellow errand-runners in line at the register. Your move?
Holiday party. You’ve been drafted as Santa’s elf — the original got sick. The costume is two sizes too small, and Santa is the chief accountant. Your move?
After the party you’re in a taxi with colleagues. The driver finds out where you work and starts complaining that your company never delivered his order. What do you do?
Evening of the company picnic. A full grill of kebabs is left, and everyone’s being loaded onto the bus. The driver is rushing you. Your move?
right: Leave them, run for the bus

text: Office party night. An AI photo bot makes “period portraits.” It painted you as a peasant hauling a sack of reports, and the CEO as a king. Print it?
9 a.m. In an hour you have a meeting with the boss that you yourself titled “Discuss my growth.” In the elevator you rehearse the line “I’m worth more.” Don’t chicken out?
right: Go in and name a number

text: You ask for a raise. The boss nods and pulls out a sheet of paper: “Let’s list your strengths first.” The sheet is blank, and you’re holding the pen. Start writing?
8:10 a.m. Mom on the phone: “Asking for a raise today? Tell them your mom is a pensioner.” Mom works and earns more than you. Your reply?
You ask accounting for market salary data — for your raise talk. They laugh: “Wrong department, try a fortune teller.” What next?
right: Go in with “I just want it”

text: 10:20. The boss raises it himself: “I know you’re waiting for a promotion. First Project Phoenix, then we’ll talk.” Phoenix has been on fire for three years. Agree?
right: Ask for a timeline in writing

text: Your desk neighbor advises asking for a 40% raise, “to leave room for haggling.” He did exactly that and now works at another company. Follow his advice?
6:30 p.m. The boss agrees to a raise, but “starting the first day of next quarter.” Today is the second day of this quarter. Ask why not now?
HR sends a “Compensation Review Request” form. The “Justification” field allows 200 characters. Your justification doesn’t even fit in the title. How will you trim it?
Lyosha heard you’re asking for a raise and wants you to “put in a good word” for him while you’re at it. He closed zero tasks this quarter. Will you?
left: Put in a word to be polite

text: You’ve put off the money talk for three months. Your inner voice suggests messaging the boss right now, at 9 p.m., while you’re feeling brave. Send it?
The boss at your raise meeting: “Money isn’t everything. How about a chair with armrests instead?” Your chair has been missing an armrest for a year. Your choice?
The CFO catches you in the hallway: “Heard you’re asking for a raise. Do you know how much your chair costs the company?” He genuinely wants to do the math. Listen?
Practice at home: your partner plays the boss and answers everything with “the budget is frozen.” Round seven, and you’re losing. One more round?
The team chat agrees to ask for raises “as a united front” at 11 a.m. So far the front consists of you and the cat on Olya’s avatar. Go?
The boss replies to your raise request: “We’ll revisit this once the company reaches a plateau.” You don’t know what the plateau is. Apparently neither does he. Ask?
At dinner a friend advises: “Bring the boss printouts of job ads that pay more.” Bold move or borderline blackmail?
The boss approved your raise! The email says plus 3%. The news that same day: inflation is 8%. Reply “thanks”?
You happen to be alone in the elevator with the CEO. Fourteen floors. Just enough time to say your salary is long overdue for a raise. Risk it?
7 p.m. The boss writes: “About your raise — I have good news, I’ll tell you Monday.” Monday is a long way off. Can you hold out?
At the salary meeting HR shows the pay band for your role. You’re at the very bottom, and the only person ever at the top left a year ago. Your response?
The head of marketing invites you over: “It’s more fun here — beanbags and Friday pizza.” Your boss doesn’t know yet. Go for an “intro coffee”?
You applied for an internal transfer. HR clarifies: “We’re required to notify your manager.” The notification goes out in a minute. Withdraw?
You moved to a new department, but your old boss keeps sending tasks in the evenings: “You know that spreadsheet anyway.” It’s 7:40 p.m. Reply?
left: Do it for old times’ sake

text: Logistics offers a transfer: same pay, but the office is two minutes from your home. You’d have to learn the waybills from scratch, though. Make the move?
The boss found out you’re eyeing another department and asks, hurt: “What, you’re unhappy here?” Your photo from the office party is on his desk. Your answer?
Analytics is ready to take you on, but first a test assignment: “A small one, about twenty hours.” Spend every evening this week on it?
First day in the new department. Here everyone eats lunch at exactly noon, together, in silence. You’re used to eating at 2 p.m. at your monitor. Join them?
Your old team throws you a farewell party as you move one floor up. The cake says “Traitor (just kidding).” The parentheses are very small. Go?
The sales director wants to poach you and is haggling with your boss. In exchange for you, he’s offering two interns and a printer. Offended?
During the transfer you learn your title in the new department is “Junior Specialist.” Same duties, more humiliating nameplate. Sign?
Your new manager sent a 60-item “onboarding checklist.” Item 1: “Read items 2–60.” Start tonight?
The next department invites you for a “one-week trial” to see if you like it. Nobody will cover your tasks meanwhile. Go?
A colleague from your old department complains: “Since you left, nobody cleans the coffee machine.” He’s hinting you could drop by. Will you?
In the evening your dream job appears on the internal portal, in another department. Requirements: everything you can do, plus Japanese. Apply?
The boss himself suggests you move to another department: “You’ll find it more interesting there.” Suspiciously, he’s looking for a spot for a new desk. Agree?
In quality control, where you just moved, there’s a tradition: the newbie spends a week checking others’ reports for commas. They’ve brought you a stack as tall as your monitor. Start?
A friend says an internal move is “like a divorce, except you keep living with your exes.” The decisive transfer meeting is tomorrow. Cancel it?
The transfer dragged on: for a month you’ve belonged to two departments at once. Both bosses set stand-ups at 9:30 at opposite ends of the building. Where do you run?
After the transfer, HR asks for your old badge. The new one takes two weeks, and the old one doesn’t open the new department’s door. What now?
left: Wait for colleagues at the door
right: Work from a café for two weeks

text: 8:40 a.m. A headhunter calls: “I have a unique position for you.” You’re on a crowded minibus, and your boss is standing right next to you. Talk?
A recruiter messages: “Saw your profile, you’re amazing!” Further down he calls you by someone else’s name. Reply?
8:15 p.m. The headhunter asks how much you earn now. You’re embarrassed to tell even your mom. What will you say?
The headhunter invites you for an “informal coffee” at the café across from the office. That café has a perfect view of your department. And vice versa. Go?
left: Go, sit back to the window

text: A recruiter sends a job posting: “Perfect fit for you!” It’s your own company, your own position. The pay is slightly higher. Interested?
right: Show the email to the boss

text: A headhunter calls mid-meeting. You step out, and he immediately asks: “Ready to relocate to another city?” The meeting goes on without you. Keep listening?
In the evening, twelve recruiters in a row add you on a professional network. Looks like someone who quit left them your contact. Accept them all?
The headhunter reassures you: “Your current employer is our client too, but don’t worry.” You start to worry. Keep talking?
Rita whispers: “A headhunter called asking about you. I said you’re the best.” Now she feels awkward, and you’re curious. Ask her more?
The headhunter sent a 180-question personality test. Question 47: “If you were a vegetable, which would you be?” You’re in the kitchen next to an eggplant. Continue?
The headhunter calls for the third time this week: the job is “urgent,” the client is “willing to do anything.” You’re only willing to have coffee. Tell the truth?
The headhunter offers one and a half times your salary but won’t name the company: “It’s a surprise.” Go to a blind interview?
9:30 p.m. The headhunter asks you to recommend “a colleague who isn’t afraid of change.” You know exactly who’s secretly job hunting. Tip him off?
The headhunter offers a “trial workday” at another company this very Friday. You’d need a day off. Take one for “family reasons”?
The IT guy confides: “The mail filter flags the word ‘vacancy.’” You’ve got seven such emails in your inbox. Clean up?
A headhunter calls your landline, a number only your grandma knows. He’s polite and somehow knows you love fishing. Talk?
You updated your job-site profile at 7:30 a.m., and by 9:00 the boss had already liked it. What does that mean?
left: Write him: “It’s not what it looks like”

text: The headhunter asks why you want to leave. You don’t — you just answered the phone. He’s already noted: “burnout.” Correct him?
A recruiter friend at dinner: “Go to an interview, just to learn your market value.” It’s tomorrow at 9 a.m., and you have stand-up. Go?
8:50 a.m. An offer from a competitor: 30% more pay, office on the outskirts, an hour and a half commute. You’ve read it five times. Accept?
You show the boss a competitor’s offer. He stares at it a long time: “Give me till Friday, I’ll talk to upper management.” Friday is far away. Wait?
7:30 p.m. The competitor’s HR wants your answer by midnight: “Otherwise the offer expires.” You haven’t talked to your boss yet. Decide now?
The boss learned about the offer and counters: the same amount plus “the right to pick the office music.” Sounds generous. Accept?
Somehow the whole department knows about your offer. In the kitchen they ask who gets your monitor. You haven’t decided anything. How to react?
At home you discuss the competitor’s offer. Your partner made a two-page pros-and-cons table. “Nice elevator” is listed under pros. Read to the end?
The competitor’s HR asks for an income statement “to understand your level.” Your accounting issues it and will definitely ask why. Request it?
At the final interview, they ask: “Tell us about your current company’s weaknesses.” The interviewer writes down every word. Be honest?
A former colleague who went to a competitor writes: “Come join us, the coffee machine makes lattes.” You know he gets a bonus per referral. Reply?
The boss got your resignation letter and silently put it in a drawer: “I never saw this. Think it over till lunch.” What now?
