right: Put a copy on his desk

text: The CEO calls you in personally: “Heard about the offer. What would it take for you to stay?” Seems you can name anything. What do you ask for?
You accepted the competitor’s offer, and an hour later panic hits: “What if it’s worse there?” You can still write that you changed your mind. Write it?
The competitor wants you to sign a paper promising not to bring “a single outside idea.” All your ideas are in your head. Sign?
Instead of a report, you accidentally pasted the competitor’s offer into the work chat. Deleted in 10 seconds. “Seen by 14.” What next?
The competitor invites you to “meet your future team” — bowling at 8 p.m. You haven’t signed the offer yet. Go?
8 a.m. Mom heard about the offer: “Good people don’t job-hop.” A minute later she calls back: “But if they pay more — run.” Whose advice do you take?
After learning about the offer, the boss suddenly addresses you with formal respect and praises your reports at stand-up. Colleagues side-eye. Accept the attention?
9 p.m. Your future boss at the competitor already added you to their work chat, though you start in a month. There’s a crisis, and everyone’s tagging you. Reply?
HR asks you to fill out an exit questionnaire. Question 3: “What would make you stay?” The answer “money” is already filled in, in someone else’s handwriting. Keep it?
Half-year goal review. The first goal on your list: “Implement the new CRM.” The CRM was canceled in March, but the goal stayed. How do you rate it?
You open the goals spreadsheet: someone changed your goal “Cut costs by 5%” to “by 50%.” The edit history says: the boss. Ask?
6:40 p.m. Before you leave, the boss asks you to “quickly” write SMART goals for the quarter. All you remember of SMART is the S. Write them?
HR sends the review form: rate each goal from “exceeded expectations” to “room to grow.” No other options. What do you give yourself?
At the goal review the boss says: “You did everything, but without a spark.” Spark isn’t mentioned in any goal. Argue about the spark?
The night before the review. Rereading your goals, you realize three of the five were done by your colleague Dima; you just helped. How do you present it?
Review in an hour. The tracker says you closed 214 tasks. 180 of them are “reply to email.” Show it like that?
A colleague suggests a “swap” for the review: he claims your report, you claim his presentation. “Everyone does it.” Agree?
The boss writes at 8 p.m.: “Looked at your goals. Why isn’t there a single one about personal growth?” Add something about growth right now?
Your goal review is run by a division director who’s seeing you for the first time. He asks: “So what do you do here?” Where to start?
HR reports: after the review you got “meets expectations.” Bonuses only go to those who “exceed.” Dispute it?
At home you’re preparing your speech for tomorrow’s review. Your partner says to use “I,” not “we”: “You did it all yourself!” Rewrite the speech?
The boss proposes an ambitious annual goal: double the numbers. Resources promised: “the same, only less.” Sign up?
Before the review Sveta asks how you describe failures. She writes “areas for discovery.” Borrow her phrasing?
9 p.m. The evaluation system closes at midnight. 9 of 10 fields done; “Your mission” remains. The site logs you out every five minutes. Finish it?
At the review the boss mistakenly opened last year’s goals instead of this year’s. By those, you’re flawless. Stay quiet?
Individual goals in the department are assigned by lottery. You drew “Raise the department’s visibility.” What does that even mean?
The goal review ran till 7 p.m., and the boss suggests continuing “at a café, my treat.” There are two more hours of questions. Go?
The goal tracker sent a reminder: “You’ve completed 3% of your goal. Smile!” Today is the last day of the quarter. How to react?
Vanya, the intern you mentor, found a mistake in your formula and quietly fixed it. He told only you. Credit him at stand-up?
Dasha, your mentee, sent a five-year development plan at 7 a.m. Item 4: “Take the mentor’s job.” The mentor is you. How to react?
An intern writes at 10 p.m.: “Sorry, I have an existential question about work.” The question: should he even work in an office. Answer now?
The boss wants your mentee “at full productivity” by Friday. The mentee is nineteen and in his second week. Promise it?
Your former mentee now earns more than you. He calls in the evening: “Can I ask your advice? How do I ask for a raise?” Help him?
Your mentee Liza writes down your every word. Today she logged “ugh, not again” in her notebook as an “important principle.” Correct her?
right: Let it stand as a principle

text: Your mentee gave his first client presentation. The client is happy, and the slides are full of your jokes — uncredited. Tell him?
You have two mentees, and both want a meeting at 10 a.m. Each is sure you like her best. Whom do you pick?
Your own mentor from the next department admits, after a year of meetings, that he still doesn’t get what you do. Keep meeting?
Your intern’s last day. She asks for a reference letter “in French, so it looks impressive.” Your French is from high school. Risk it?
right: Write a warm one in English

text: HR introduces mentor KPIs: “percentage of mentees who stay with the company.” Your only mentee said yesterday he’s leaving. Talk him out of it?
Your mentee asks why you’re not a boss yet if you know everything. He genuinely doesn’t understand. Neither do you. Your answer?
6:50 p.m. Intern Grisha sent a 23-page report for review and is waiting for feedback “today, please.” Review it?
At stand-up your mentee passes off your idea as her own. The boss praises it. She looks at you in horror. What do you do?
The company launches “reverse mentoring”: an intern teaches you new apps. First assignment: film a dance video. Participate?
A former mentee invites you to speak at his new company: “Tell them how you trained me.” Friday at 7 p.m. Agree?
Your mentee came to your meeting with a list of 30 questions. Question 1: “How do you handle stress?” Your eye starts twitching. Answer?
The boss suggests giving your best mentee to another department “as reinforcement.” In return he promises a new one, “still fresh.” Agree?
Your mentee writes: “Thanks for teaching me! I passed the interview at a competitor.” Your boss doesn’t know who trained him yet. Congratulate him?
right: Ask him to leave you out of it

text: 9:01 a.m. Company email: “Congratulations to Artyom on his appointment as team lead!” You’ve been preparing for that role for six months. Artyom sits across from you. What do you do?
Artyom, a colleague until yesterday and now your manager, asks you for the first time to “prepare a status update by four.” He used to ask to borrow your charger. Do it?
The department is celebrating Katya’s promotion at a bar. The promotion you were up for. Everyone’s making toasts, and yours is expected too. Go?
The boss explains why you weren’t promoted: “You’re too valuable where you are.” So you’ve been punished for doing good work. Ask about the logic?
Freshly minted manager Dima asks your advice on how to manage. You’d like to manage yourself. Give advice?
In the evening you look at the profile of the colleague who got promoted. It says “strategic thinker.” You remember him spending a week trying to recall his email password. What next?
HR sends a survey: “How do you rate the decision to promote your colleague?” Anonymous — but with your employee number in the header. Be honest?
The team chat is flooded with stickers for Olya’s promotion. The only ones who haven’t reacted: you and the cleaner who got added by mistake. Send a sticker?
Your partner asks why you’re so gloomy. Reason: a colleague got promoted and you didn’t. Your partner offers tea, cake and venting. Accept?
Your deskmate got promoted, is moving to an office and asks you to carry her ficus. The ficus is heavier than your resentment. Carry it?
The boss offers a “consolation prize” for not getting promoted: a window seat. The window faces the wall of the next building. Take it?
Tanya, who got promoted, writes at 9 p.m.: “Can I sometimes come to you for advice? You understand this stuff better.” Your reply?
At morning stand-up they announce Gosha’s promotion. Everyone applauds, and you’re holding hot coffee. How do you clap?
right: Raise the mug as a toast

text: Vika, promoted instead of you, invites you to lunch “like old times.” Only now, at lunch, she asks about your deadlines. Go?
The HR bot congratulates you: “You’ve been promoted!” A minute later, a correction: “Sorry, this message was sent to the wrong employee.” Reply to the bot?
The CEO hands the promoted colleague a certificate, mixing up his surname with yours. The room laughs. The CEO looks at you: “And who are you?” Your answer?
In the smoking area people whisper that Petya got promoted because he plays tennis with the boss. You’re invited to discuss it over coffee. Join?
In the evening you list all the ways you’re better than the person who got promoted. It runs two pages. Send the list to the boss?
right: Tear it up and toss it

text: A former colleague, now your boss, holds your first one-on-one. He’s clearly read a management book: maintains eye contact and nods every three seconds. Can you handle it?
9:20 a.m. Whispers in the smoking area: “They’re cutting one in five.” You do the math: ten people in the department, two were late today. You’re one of them. What now?
The word “optimization” appeared in the chat, and a minute later everyone deleted their messages. Only your “??” remains. Delete it too?
A friend from accounting writes in the evening: “Can’t say anything, but update your résumé.” Plus three skull emojis. Update it now?
Consultants in identical jackets have appeared. One sits by your desk and writes down everything you do. How do you work?
Asked about layoffs, the boss replies: “No one will be laid off. Except those who will.” And goes to lunch. What to do with this info?
You search “how to survive layoffs.” Tip #1: “Know the password to everything.” You only know the printer password. Is that enough?
HR booked a 15-minute meeting with you at 11 a.m. with no description. In the calendar it’s titled “Conversation.” Wait or go ask now?
The “conversation” with HR was about new parking rules. You spent two hours bracing for the worst. Treat yourself to leaving early?
Oleg proposes a “survival pact”: if one gets cut, the other brings him cookies and forwards job ads. Sign it on a napkin?
The meeting room door has a sign: “Reorganization.” From inside: “Do we even need this department?” Is it yours?
The CEO emails everyone: “Rumors of layoffs are false.” Last time such an email came a week before layoffs. Believe it?
At home you mention the layoff rumors. Your partner suggests that “just in case” you stop buying cheese. Cheese is your main joy in life. Economize?
The IT guy approaches with a box: “Is this your monitor?” Turns out it’s just a replacement. But your heart is already in your shoes. Reaction?
The anonymous company channel says they’ll cut “people who eat loudly.” You just opened a bag of chips. Keep eating?
left: One chip at a time, quietly

text: 7:40 p.m. The boss suddenly advises you to save your work files to a USB drive “just in case.” He says it’s “for good order.” Ask what it means?
Someone left a “Key Employees” list on the printer. You’re not on it. The coffee machine is, as “key equipment.” What now?
The team lead asks everyone to describe “your contribution in one sentence” — “to understand the structure.” Everyone knows the real reason. What do you write?
The department decided to go out after work for a “last supper, just in case.” Nobody’s been cut yet. Go?
The new Director of Efficiency walks around asking everyone: “What happens if tomorrow you’re not here?” Your answer?
9:10 a.m. Sasha’s desk is empty, his computer’s off, his mug is gone. Silence in chat. You were the last to see him yesterday at 6 p.m. Text him?
The boss announces Lena was fired and her projects are now yours. All five. Lena took the passwords with her. Call Lena?
Maxim, fired yesterday, invites you to a bar: “I’ll tell you how it really went down.” The boss would also love to know what he says. Go?
The office manager says you can take a keepsake from a laid-off colleague’s desk — the rest gets tossed. There’s a cat-shaped stapler and a cactus. Which do you take?
The department is collecting for a farewell gift for laid-off Igor. The idea: a tie “for interviews.” Chip in?
Laid-off Vadim asks you to write him a reference “as his manager,” since the manager won’t reply. You’re not his manager. Help?
The boss asks you not to tell anyone Zoya was fired “until we announce it.” Zoya texts you: “Any idea why my badge isn’t working?” Reply?
HR asks you to speak at a laid-off colleague’s farewell “on behalf of the team.” He’s leaving amid a scandal and is angry at everyone. Will you speak?
right: Pass the mic to someone else

text: Laid-off Marina left every chat except the one with you. Late at night she writes: “I think it was because of you.” You did nothing. Reply?
A newcomer already sits at laid-off Kostya’s desk. He asks why the monitor has a sticky note: “If Kostya gets fired, call Ira.” Explain?
Nina was laid off and is giving away everything — from pens to a jar of coffee. You got her unfinished report for the boss. Also a “gift”?
In the evening you realize the colleague laid off today was the only one who knew how the annual report gets compiled. It’s due in a week. What do you do?
The boss asks which of two interns to keep after probation. One is diligent, the other is funny. You’re expected to be honest. Which one?
A colleague laid off a month ago came to collect his work papers, but security won’t let him in. He waves to you through the glass. Go meet him?
The laid-off team lead started a blog: “How I Survived This Office.” In the third post, you appear under the code name “The Quiet One.” Subscribe?
In the morning you learn Petya was laid off — the guy who always bought cookies for the team. No more cookies. Someone has to step up. You?
The company lawyer asks you to confirm that fired Gleb was “systematically late.” Gleb was late. But so were you. Sign?
Anya, laid off six months ago, writes: “I earn twice as much now. Thanks for not defending me back then.” Joke or reproach?
The security guard whispers: “Last night they deactivated badges for two people in your department.” He doesn’t know whose. Check yours?
9 a.m. The annual bonuses were supposed to arrive today. Your account: zero. Accounting’s auto-reply: “On vacation until the 15th.” What now?
The boss explains the bonus delay: “The money exists, but it’s somewhere else.” He doesn’t say where. Ask?
You’d mentally spent your bonus on a vacation, but it’s been delayed. Your partner has packed the suitcases and asks if the trip is still on. Confess?
HR sends the bonus formula: “Salary × coefficient × manager’s mood index.” The boss’s index has been low since morning. Bring him coffee?
Bonuses arrived, and the team is comparing amounts in chat. Yours is suspiciously large. Everyone’s waiting for you to post yours. Confess?
You got your bonus this evening. Mom on the phone, oh-so-casually: “Anything come your way at work?” Confess?
The CFO at the all-hands: “Bonuses will be paid in company shares.” Internal shares — which you can only sell to the CFO himself. Sign up?
The accountant says your bonus “got lost in the migration to the new system.” It’ll turn up if you dig out an order from two years ago. Search?
Misha tells you in secret that only your department’s bonuses were delayed: “Ours came yesterday.” Take this to the boss tomorrow?
7:45 a.m., team chat: “Bonuses are in!!!” Yours isn’t. A minute later the author writes: “Oops, I dreamed it.” Your reply?
The boss offers a “non-monetary bonus”: your photo on the “Employee of the Month” board. They’ll use your badge photo. Agree?
right: Ask for a chocolate at least

text: 6:55 p.m. Accounting: “Anyone who doesn’t sign the bonus form by 7:00 gets it next year.” The form is on the fifth floor; you’re on the first. Run?
HR announces this year’s bonuses are “flexible”: cash, vacation days or a pool membership. Your pick?
The project bonus is split “by contribution,” decided by a team vote. You worked quietly for three weeks, never posting updates in chat. What now?
You open your banking app for the fifth time this hour. The bonus was promised “by end of day.” Accounting’s end of day is a stretchy concept. Once more?
The CEO thanks everyone by email for a record year. One paragraph down: bonuses are postponed “due to investment in the future.” Reply?
right: Discuss it in the smoking area

text: The accountant hands out your bonus in cash in an envelope, “to be faster.” The envelope has someone else’s name, but the amount looks like yours. Take it?
You got your bonus and took the department to a restaurant. The bill arrives — exactly equal to your bonus. To the cent. Pay it all?
The team lead announces bonuses go to those who hit 120% of their goal. Your goal was set last Friday, and today is the last day of the period. What now?
The team bonus is a Saturday trip to a resort. You’d planned to sleep all Saturday. Declining means you’re “not a team player.” Go?
8:30 a.m. An acquaintance offers a side gig: designing menus for his café in the evenings. Pays in pizza and money. Mostly pizza. Take it?
The boss sees a spreadsheet on your screen: “Private client orders.” It’s your side gig, during work hours. He’s coming closer. What do you do?
9 p.m. A side-gig client sends edits: “Make the logo more summery.” It’s October. Take it on?
Borya found out you host weddings on weekends and asks you to host his “for free, as a friend.” Two hundred guests. Agree?
HR sends a reminder: “Unapproved side work is a violation.” For a year you’ve been translating washing machine manuals in the evenings. Confess?
You’re editing a video for a side gig, eyes closing. Three hours to the deadline, six to your alarm. Keep going?
Your neighbor found out you work “in an office with computers” and offers to pay you to set up his router. Right now, before work. You’d be twenty minutes late. Help?
A colleague confesses he drives a taxi in the evenings and offers to drive you home “at cost.” He doesn’t say how much that is. Accept?
An online school invites you to teach in the evenings: “Show students how to work with spreadsheets.” Classes on Thursdays until 10 p.m. Agree?
You started selling knitted mug cozies — the dream side hustle. By 9 a.m. the first four orders came in. All from colleagues. Give “friends” a discount?
Your side-gig client turned out to be a client of your company. At a meeting he winks at you. The boss notices. Wink back?
A friend invites you to help with moving jobs on weekends: “Good money and a workout.” Saturday’s list: two couches and a piano. Sign up?
On a team call, your laptop’s “Recent files” reveals your side gig: “Side_job_final_FINAL.” Everyone had time to read it. What now?
Kira proposes a joint business: selling homemade salads to colleagues at lunch. Her salads are delicious. But lunch is your only rest. Join?
In the evening it dawns on you that side-gig income is taxable, and you’ve never filed a tax return. The tax website is open. Start?
Your houseplant blog started making money. An advertiser expects a ficus post by 11 a.m., and you’re in a meeting until noon. Write it during the meeting?
The boss found out you draw commissions and asks for a portrait of his mother-in-law “as a favor, free.” Deadline: her birthday on Saturday. Draw it?
You did the math for the first time: the side gig earns almost as much as your job but eats every evening. An order is waiting right now. Rest just once?
Bank statement: side-gig income this month — $30, transfer fees — $10. Keep this business going?
7:30 a.m. Instead of exercising, you’re again coding your pet project — an app that counts how many times a day you yawn. Be late for a commit?
The IT guy notices your pet project is running on the office server: “I won’t tell anyone, but space is running out.” What now?
Your pet project — a recipe site for the office microwave — hit a thousand visitors. Colleagues recognized themselves in the recipe “Sergei’s Fish.” Rename it?
The boss learned about your pet project and offers to “make it part of your job.” Then the company would own the rights. Gift or trap?
Stas wants in on your pet project: “I’ll generate ideas.” You, apparently, will write the code. Bring him on?
9 p.m. You have seven unfinished pet projects. An idea for an eighth just struck — better than all the others. Start right now?
An email from an “investor”: he wants to buy your pet project for a fortune — you just need to pay a “registration fee.” What do you do?
right: Forward it to colleagues for laughs

text: For the third day in a row you spend lunch on your pet project, eating over the keyboard. Colleagues invite you to a café again. Go at least today?
Your partner asks when you last ate dinner away from the laptop. The pet project has been “almost done” for three months. Close the laptop?
Your pet project — a birthday reminder bot — wished everyone a happy birthday to the accountant. His birthday is in May. Fix it in front of everyone?
At a demo the boss presents “a new in-house tool.” It’s your pet project, which you showed him a week ago. Your name isn’t mentioned. Raise your hand?
Your pet project made the finals of a startup contest. The final is Wednesday at 3 p.m., during work hours. Take a day off?
Your pet project crashed at 6 a.m., and all twelve users are writing angry reviews. You have a meeting at 10. Fix it from your phone on the subway?
Vera uses your lunch-planner app and asks for “one tiny feature”: account for her diet. Her diet changes daily. Add it?
The lawyer writes: per your contract, anything you create “at any hour of the day” belongs to the company. Your pet project is a borscht recipe site. The borscht too?
right: Delete the project, just in case

text: The CEO subscribed to your pet project — under a nickname, but with his photo as the avatar. You noticed over dinner. What now?
The team lead saw you talk about your pet project at a meetup and asks why you’re not this fired up at work. Fair point. Your answer?
You did the math: the pet project costs $40 a month in hosting and earns 50 cents. Your only subscriber writes “thank you.” Keep going?
You asked colleagues to test your pet project. In one evening: 40 bugs, half signed “just kidding, but not really.” Read them all?
PR invites you to speak at a meetup on behalf of the company. The boss hints it “will count at the salary review.” Agree?
Rehearsing your talk for the team. You’re on slide two, and colleagues are already asking if there’ll be a coffee break. Cut the talk in half?
9:30 p.m. You’re rehearsing your talk for the tenth time in the bathroom mirror. The neighbor bangs on the wall: “We get it, synergy!” One more run?
You arrived at the conference at 9 a.m., and your talk was moved from 3 p.m. to 9:15. The slides are on a laptop at home. What now?
Mid-talk, a hand goes up: “Not so much a question as a comment.” The comment is entering its fourth minute. Interrupt?
6:30 p.m. The CEO: “Tomorrow at the shareholders’ meeting you’ll say a few words on behalf of the staff.” How many is “a few”? And what do you say to shareholders?
You step on stage: the mic is handheld, the clicker is in your other hand, and you also have a paper with your speech. No third hand. What do you drop?
right: Put the clicker on the floor

text: A recording of your talk was posted on the corporate portal. The thumbnail shows you with eyes closed and mouth open. Ask to change it?
Colleagues came to support you at an evening meetup and sat in the front row with a sign: “We love you.” You hoped to present unnoticed. What now?
The boss asks you to open the department all-hands with a speech: “You have such a good speaking voice.” You have the voice, but no speech. Agree?
After your talk someone asks: “What will you do if the approach doesn’t work?” You’ve never once thought about it. Your answer?
You’re invited as a guest on an industry podcast. Recording at 8 p.m. from home. At home: a cat, a neighbor’s hammer drill and a washing machine on spin. Agree?
The conference host introduces you as “an expert with twenty years of experience.” You’ve worked for six. Correct him?
The clicker froze, and the organizer changes slides when you say “Next.” He’s two slides behind. Carry on like this?
The recording of your meetup talk went online. 300 comments, all discussing your shirt, not your talk. Reply?
HR paid for a public speaking course for you. Evening classes; first assignment: tell strangers about your childhood. Go tonight?
Before your talk you spot a typo on a slide: “Revenue growth of 300%.” It should be 3%. The CEO is already in the room. Correct it out loud?
Friends are watching your talk’s livestream and posting in the public chat: “That’s our friend!!!” Everyone can see the chat. How to react?
A competitor speaks right before you and presents exactly what’s on your slides. Word for word. You’re up in five minutes. What now?
At the buffet after your successful talk, the boss tells everyone “he taught you everything.” You’ve only seen him at talks asleep. Object?
Veronika returned your report with a note: “Paragraph spacing is 1.15, not 1.1.” The report already went to the boss. Recall the email and redo it?
For the third hour, Veronika has been nudging the logo on a slide “two pixels to the left.” The deck can’t go out without her slide. What do you do?
7:10 p.m. Veronika asks you to stay and “go over the commas one last time” in a contract that’s been proofread three times. Stay?
Overnight Veronika restructured the shared drive: 14 levels of folders, all color-coded. The links in your client emails are broken. Your reaction?
Veronika found a cell in your spreadsheet with a slightly different shade of gray and called a mini-meeting about it. Go?
At 9 p.m. Veronika posts in chat: “Noticed the email template has a period after the signature. Is that even okay?” The chat is silent. Reply?
9:40 a.m. Stas writes: “Be there in five minutes.” His third “five minutes” since 9:00. Stand-up can’t start without him — he’s presenting. What now?
Stas was 25 minutes late to a client lunch and asks you to confirm you “got stuck in the elevator together.” Will you?
Stas bursts in at 10:20 with two coffees: one for you, “so you’ll cover for me with the boss if needed.” Take the coffee?
Stas suggests coming in early tomorrow, at 8 a.m., “to surprise everyone.” He asks you to call and wake him at 7. Agree?
The boss asks in front of everyone: “Where’s Stas? Anyone know?” You do: Stas just texted you he’s still at home. Answer honestly?
Stas returns from lunch at 3:10: “You didn’t start the call without me, right?” You started it and already finished. Fill him in?
Gena hands out pedometers to the whole department: “Anyone under 10,000 steps buys fruit for everyone.” In?
Gena puts a green spinach-ginger smoothie on your desk: “It replaces your pastry. You’ll thank me later.” Try it?
right: Give it back, eat the pastry

text: Gena suggests holding stand-ups in a plank position: “They’ll get shorter instantly!” The boss nods thoughtfully. Support it?
6:30 p.m. Gena invites the department for an evening run around the business center “for team spirit.” Eight laps. Go?
At lunch Gena counts the calories on your plate out loud: “Whoa, that’s half a day at the gym.” Your reply?
At 8:30 Gena opens every window: “Oxygen is brain fuel!” It’s 37°F outside, and you’re in a shirt. What do you do?
Gena replaced the coffee cream in the shared fridge with oat milk: “You’ll thank me.” The department grumbled. Your stance?
Gena invites you to his birthday at 8 p.m.: “No cake — there’ll be a detox set and meditation.” Go?
8:05 a.m. Larisa sent twelve voice messages in a row, the longest 4:37. In text, the answer to your question would be “yes.” Listen to them all?
Larisa is recording a voice message right by your desk, though she could just say it to you. The message is for you. How to react?
8:40 p.m. Larisa sends a voice message: “Don’t listen now, listen tomorrow.” Length: 9:12. What do you do?
At stand-up Larisa plays a client’s six-minute voice message from her phone: “It’s more accurate this way.” The whole team listens to street noise. What do you do?
You got a voice message from Larisa. The first two minutes are her chatting with a cashier. Then the connection drops. Reply?
Larisa asks you to record a voice message for her mom: “Say I’m in a meeting — she’ll believe you.” Record it?
“Just a quick question,” says Zinaida from procurement, sitting in your chair. Her third question this morning, none about procurement. What do you do?
right: Get up and go for coffee

text: Zinaida pops in: “Just a quick question — have you had lunch?” She’s holding a bag of pastries and clearly wants to discuss a report. Let her in?
6:55 p.m., jacket on. Zinaida at the elevator: “Just a quick question, won’t take long.” The question is about HR policy since 2014. Answer?
A courier calls from the lobby: “Just a quick question — did you really order 40 chairs?” You didn’t. But someone did. Accept them?
Every ten minutes your desk neighbor turns around: “Can I ask a dumb question?” Fourteen so far today. What do you do?
Arkady invited thirty-two people to a 9 a.m. meeting, including some who quit a year ago. You’re the only one who accepted. Go?
Arkady schedules an hour-and-a-half meeting: “Discuss how to reduce the number of meetings.” You’re marked as required. Go?
The calendar shows Arkady booked you for “Weekly Retro” on Friday at 6 p.m. That’s your rightful time to go home. What do you do?
Arkady created a recurring meeting for the rest of the year, daily at 11 a.m. It’s called “Quick Sync.” What do you do?
Arkady canceled a meeting a minute before it started and immediately booked a new one at the same time with a different title. What do you do?
Arkady asks you to take meeting minutes “on a permanent basis.” Nobody reads the minutes, but everyone demands them. Agree?
Arkady moves your client meeting to “free up the slot” for his own stand-up. The client already confirmed. What now?
Budget battle: marketing wants more for the office party than your department got for the whole year. The finance guy asks your opinion in chat. What do you write?
The CFO is cutting budgets: “Whichever department submits its estimate first gets more.” The estimate has 40 lines. Start right away?
7:20 p.m. Your boss asks you to “pad” the estimate by 20% — “they’ll cut it anyway.” You’re the one signing it. What do you do?
IT offers to swap your two monitors for its coffee machine budget. Your team objects, but you’re already dreaming of coffee. Trade?
Sales proposes an alliance: “Vote for our budget, and we’ll give you the meeting room on Wednesdays.” Make the deal?
You booked the meeting room for 2 p.m., but accounting is in there: “We’ve been here since 1 and will be indefinitely.” What do you do?
6 p.m. Someone booked the main meeting room for the entire next quarter as “Reserved.” Want to find out who?
The office manager introduces a “meeting room auction”: whoever posts in chat first at 8 a.m. gets it. Will you wake up at 7:55?
In the only quiet meeting room, Gena is running a meditation session. You have a client call in five minutes. What now?
5:40 p.m. The “Baikal” meeting room has three leftover pizzas from someone’s meeting and nobody around. Your meeting starts in 20 minutes. The pizza?
The meeting room door says “Occupied. Important!” but inside, a logistics manager is asleep. You have a booking. Wake him?
Reception informs you: your department lost the “Elbrus” meeting room — “temporarily” given to legal for six months. Fight it?
A deadline was missed. The boss asks: “Who was responsible for the timeline?” Your intern was — but you assigned him. Everyone’s staring at the floor. Your move?
At stand-up it turns out a client received someone else’s invoice. Three people sent invoices, and each is sure it wasn’t him. You’re not sure. Confess?
7 p.m. The chat erupts: “Who deleted the mockups folder?” You didn’t, but you were the last one in there. Mention it?
A colleague whispers: “If they ask about the error in the report, we’ll say it was a system glitch, okay?” The error is his. Go along?
The boss himself mixed up the shipping date, and at stand-up he says: “Someone let us down.” He looks at you. What will you say?
At the retro, the facilitator asks everyone to name “their share of responsibility” for the failed release. You go first. What do you say?
In the evening a colleague writes: “Tomorrow they’ll be looking for someone to blame. Let’s agree neither of us knew.” Agree?
By the water cooler, an accountant whispers: “They say your boss is leaving and they want Arkady to replace him.” Whom will you tell?
Maya from HR proposes a friendship “against marketing”: sharing news first. In return she wants your department’s gossip. Deal?
After work two colleagues invite you to a bar and start trashing the boss. You’re new at this company. How do you behave?
Arkady quietly offers: “Back me at the meeting and I’ll put in a good word for you.” You don’t like his idea. Back him?
Sales and marketing got into a fight in the main chat. Both sides DM you asking you to “just like” their position. What do you do?
9:30 p.m. A colleague forwards you a screenshot from a chat where people say you “always drag things out.” Reply in that chat?
You overheard the next department agreeing to pin a failed delivery on you. The meeting is in an hour. What do you do?
The new guy asks: “Who’s good to be friends with here?” He’s clearly looking for a patron. Answer honestly?
left: Explain the lay of the land

text: Nina Ivanovna isn’t a boss, but every decision goes through her. Today she didn’t like your tone in chat. Go apologize?
Nina Ivanovna called the new tracking system “nonsense.” The department stopped using it. The boss asks you to bring everyone back. How?
At 6:30 p.m. Nina Ivanovna announces: “Tomorrow everyone wears blue to support Alla at her project defense.” You own nothing blue. What do you do?
Quiet Vadik from IT knows everyone’s passwords and browser histories. He asks you to help him move on Saturday. Help?
The boss asks: “Why does everyone listen to Nina Ivanovna and not me?” He expects an honest answer right now. What will you say?
The department informally chose you as its “ambassador” to management: take the AC petition to the boss. The boss is in a foul mood today. Go?
Lyova, the soul of the department, is quitting, and at 6 p.m. he asks you to take over “the people stuff”: birthdays, collections, consolations. Will you?
Gleb taped your mouse to the underside of your desk. The whole team awaits your reaction. A call with the boss starts in a minute. What do you do?
Gleb replaced the boss’s photo on the internal portal with a cat in a tie. The boss asks you who did it. Rat him out?
At 6 p.m. Gleb emails the department: “Urgent: all bonuses canceled!” — with “just kidding” in tiny print at the end. Half the team is panicking. Your reaction?
Gleb swapped the O and A keys on your keyboard. You’re typing an email to a client. Email first or revenge first?
At lunch Gleb tells the same joke for the fifth time this week. Everyone laughs politely. He looks at you. Your reaction?
Gleb wants to plant a squeaky rubber chicken on the boss’s desk. He needs an accomplice to keep watch. In?
Eduard peers at your screen: “You’re not using VLOOKUP, are you? That’s so last century.” How you calculate is your business, but he won’t leave. What do you do?
At stand-up Eduard corrects you: “It’s ‘fewer errors,’ not ‘less errors.’” He’s right, but you were reporting a failed project. Your reaction?
At 8 p.m. Eduard picks apart your presentation in chat, point by point: “Muddy colors, outdated font, shaky logic.” The boss is reading. Reply?
You finally fixed the printer. Eduard walks by: “I’d have done it simpler.” The printer jams again. Let him do it?
Eduard advises you on choosing an apartment, switching toothpaste and raising your cat. You only asked him the time. What now?
Eduard overruled your solution in front of the client: “We’ll do it differently, of course.” The client liked his proposal. Your move?
left: Agree in front of the client
right: Object in front of the client

text: In the evening Eduard asks for help: “I know how it’s done, of course, just check it.” Every other formula in the file is wrong. Tell him?
In the open-plan office, Zoya is loudly telling a friend on the phone how her date went. In detail. The department has stopped typing. What do you do?
Zoya is arguing with her bank on speakerphone: “Miss, I’ve been on hold for forty minutes!” You’re on a client call. What now?
right: Ask her to keep it down

text: Zoya loudly reads her card number over the phone to a courier. The whole department froze. The digits are out there. Say something?
Your desk neighbor talks on the phone in a whisper that carries better than a shout: “No, and I told him exactly that…” What do you do?
A manager from the next department takes all his calls pacing between your desks as if it were his office. Say something?
7:05 p.m. You call your mom, forgetting the speakerphone is on. The department learns that you “forgot your hat again.” How do you get out of this?
Before sending to the client, Veronika asks to check everything again — for the sixth time. The client has been waiting since 9 a.m. Send it yourself?
At 10 p.m. Veronika sent the “final version”: the file is named “result_final_really_final_v14.” One comma changed inside. Reply?
Veronika refuses to go home while there are empty cells in the shared spreadsheet. The empty ones are yours. It’s 6:40 p.m. What do you do?
Stas writes in the evening: “I’ll be late tomorrow, but don’t tell anyone — I’ll walk in like I’ve been there forever.” You two are teamed up on the project. Cover for him?
Stas was forty minutes late to his own going-on-vacation party. The cake melted, the team is mad. You’re hosting. Start without him?
At 8 p.m. Gena posts your lunch photo in the team chat with the caption “Don’t do this” — shawarma in the frame. Your reaction?
Gena invites the department to a Saturday “2 km swim” at the pool. You can only dog-paddle. Go?
At 11:15 p.m. Larisa sent a voice message and instantly deleted it. Now it just says “Message deleted.” Ask what it was?
Larisa runs the department’s “Friday News” chat in voice messages only. Today’s episode is 14 minutes. You’re at a pottery class. Listen?
Zinaida calls in the evening: “Just a quick question, did I wake you?” It’s 9:50 p.m., and the question is about where the stapler went. Answer?
At 7:30 p.m. Arkady pushes all your meetings tomorrow “one minute later each, to avoid overlaps.” The calendar is glowing red. What do you do?
In the evening Arkady books a meeting for Saturday at 10 a.m., “optional but encouraged.” Go?
Accounting and IT are arguing over whose budget pays for new headphones for your team. While they argue — no headphones. Buy your own?
7:45 p.m. The CFO wants every single dollar of the department budget justified by morning. The estimate has 312 lines. Start now?
The evening meeting room is booked for the “Corporate Choir.” You need 20 minutes for a call to the regional office. What do you do?
The guard says someone books the tenth-floor meeting room every evening but just goes there to sleep. Investigate?
Before leaving the boss asks: “Who sent the client a price list with a 50% discount today?” It was your draft; Gleb sent it. What will you say?
Maya from HR writes: “Just between us: they want you on the office party committee. It’s a real opportunity.” An opportunity to work evenings. Agree?
Nina Ivanovna calls in the evening: “I heard you’re not coming to Lilya’s birthday. That’s not right.” Your reply?
Gleb left early and left you a “surprise” in your desk drawer — a timer set to beep at 6:30 p.m. It’s beeping. You can’t find the off switch. Your move?
Gleb is organizing an office stand-up comedy night: “You owe me five minutes of material about accounting.” Accounting will be in the audience. Perform?
At the office party Eduard is teaching the bartender to mix cocktails “properly.” The bartender looks at you pleadingly. Intervene?
Eduard sent you a link to an article: “Why You’re Managing Tasks Wrong.” Caption: “Thought of you.” Reply?
left: Reply with a link of your own

text: At 6:30 p.m. Zoya is fighting with her husband on speakerphone about who picks up the kid. Everyone hears and is quietly packing up. You need to ask her about a report. Approach her?
On the commuter train, a colleague is loudly discussing your project on the phone, client name and all. You’re in the same car. What do you do?
The team is deciding who goes to ask the boss for a deadline extension. Everyone nominates you: “He likes you.” Go?
Stas introduced a “loyalty program”: for every three times he’s late, he treats you to a donut. Today’s a donut day. Take it?
Stas arrived on time. First time in a year. The team applauds, and the boss suspiciously asks you: “Did something happen?” Answer?
Stas is late for his own client presentation. You know the slides by heart. The client is checking the time. Present instead of him?
Gena bikes to work and dries his T-shirt on the back of your chair: “It’ll dry fast.” Your reaction?
Gena launched a “no-sugar challenge” and inspects the trash bins. You’ve hidden a chocolate bar in your drawer. Gena is heading your way. Your move?
Larisa posted a voice message in the main work chat: “Guys, is everything still on?” Nobody knows what “everything” is. Ask in chat?
Larisa asks you to transcribe her voice message for a client: “Can you believe he doesn’t listen to voice messages?” It’s 11 minutes long. Do it?
Zinaida from procurement came “just to ask” and told you whose bonus will be cut this year. You’re not on the list. Yet. Ask more?
Your neighbor starts every morning with “Just a quick question” and asks for the Wi-Fi password. It hasn’t changed since spring. What do you do?
left: Stick a note on his monitor

text: Arkady invented a “pre-meeting meeting” to prepare for the client meeting. Now that one needs its own prep. Go?
right: Go straight to the main one

text: Arkady booked a “quick 15-minute call” at 8:45 a.m. with you and five people in a time zone where it’s 5:45 a.m. Join?
Marketing spent its leftover budget on a giant inflatable logo. It’s in your meeting room because “there’s nowhere else.” What now?
The CFO announced: whoever saves the most gets part of the savings for their team party. Your team suggests giving up paper. Entirely. Support it?
Logistics has taken every meeting room for “strategic sessions” until Friday. Inside: a 2,000-piece jigsaw puzzle. Complain?
You enter the meeting room you booked, and Nina Ivanovna is having tea with friends. She says: “We’ll just be five little minutes.” Wait?
Your boss lost the fight with the next department over the big meeting room. He suggests “quietly occupying it” at lunch. In?
The meeting room was renamed “Synergy Space.” Now nobody can find it in the booking system. Your meeting is in 10 minutes. What do you do?
A client is unhappy, and the boss asks who ran the project. The new guy did, but he’s on sick leave. You’re his mentor. Answer?
9:15 a.m., chat: “Who broke the coffee machine?” You did, at 8:50, by pressing all the buttons at once. Confess?
A contractor missed the deadline and asks you not to tell the boss it was his fault: “Say approvals were delayed.” Approvals are you. What do you do?
Veronika wrote the department a 47-point policy on how to title emails. Point 31 bans the word “urgent.” Sign it?
At a meeting Veronika asks to delay the launch a week: “The icon looks 3% sadder than it should.” The boss looks at you. Your say?
Veronika secretly reprinted the sticky notes on your monitor in a neat font and sorted them by color. Now you can’t find the important one. What do you do?
Veronika asks you to take “a quick look” at her report and find at least one mistake: “I can’t send it until you do.” There are none. What now?
8:59 a.m. Stas asks you to swipe him in at the turnstile with his card: “I’m two minutes away, I swear.” You’ve had his card since last week. What do you do?
Stas proposes a “flexible start time” for everyone: “I’m just a pioneer.” The boss asks for your opinion. Support it?
Your neighbor is always late and has a new excuse each morning. Today: “Geese blocked the road.” You live on the same street. There are no geese. What do you say?
Gena suggests replacing the birthday cake for the boss with a “healthy cake” of pumpkin and chia. You’re collecting the money. What do you order?
At 8 a.m. Gena is running a warm-up by the water cooler, loudly counting squats. You just wanted some water. Join?
Gena brought an exercise ball to the office and suggests you sit on it “instead of that awful chair.” Try it?
In a meeting, Larisa records a voice memo for the boss “so nothing’s forgotten” and accidentally sends it to the client chat. Only you noticed. Tell her?
A voice message in the work chat from an unknown number: “Hi, it’s me. Well, you know.” You don’t know. Neither does anyone else. What do you do?
right: Wait for it to clear up

text: Larisa learned you can speed up voice messages, so now she records them slower “so the speed-up doesn’t eat the words.” What will you say?
Zinaida came “just to ask” and has been sitting here for 40 minutes. You’re on a call, she’s right beside you. The client asks who’s talking. What do you do?
The accountant writes: “Just a quick question — why is there a $90 taxi?” You went to pick up a client from the airport. The receipt stayed in the car. What do you do?
Arkady sent a meeting invite titled “Important!!!” through a system that sends reminders every five minutes. The meeting is in three hours. What do you do?
Arkady asks why you haven’t accepted his meeting “Discussing the Discussion.” Explain honestly?
Arkady scheduled a meeting with himself, “Focus Time,” and added you as “optional.” What do you do?
Marketing and sales share one printer and wage war over the toner every morning. Today the cartridge is in your hands. Who gets it?
The CFO cut the office party budget. You’re told to choose: keep the host or keep the food. Which stays?
Someone has occupied the “Neva” meeting room with backpacks and jackets — no booking, no people. Your meeting is in a minute. What do you do?
left: Pile it all in a corner

text: Your business center now charges for meeting rooms. The boss says: “Meet in the hallway, the budget isn’t made of rubber.” The client arrives at 10. Where?
The boss demands to know who blew the project deadline: “Nobody leaves until someone names a name.” It’s 4:30 p.m. What do you do?
At the incident review it turns out everything broke because of the password “123,” set by someone on your team six months ago. You remember who. Say it?
The client wants someone to blame for a late delivery: “Who was responsible?” Stas was, but Stas is currently “five minutes away.” Your answer?
In the kitchen Maya from HR proposes swapping “interesting stuff”: she knows who applied for a transfer. You’re curious. Trade?
The sales folks invite you to lunch: “We’ll tell you something about the new structure.” They’re sitting at the rival department’s table. Go?
Arkady and Eduard are feuding. Both invite you for coffee at 9:30. Same time. Different cafés. Where do you go?
Your boss quietly asks you to compile a “dossier” on a rival department: their mistakes, deadlines, complaints. For “defense at the board meeting.” Do it?
Nina Ivanovna offers you the window seat — the very one the department has fought over for three years. On her terms: you water the plants. Take it?
Nina Ivanovna told the new hire: “Go ask over there, they’ll explain everything,” and pointed at you. You know nothing about her task. What now?
right: Send her back to Nina Ivanovna

text: Morning chat poll: “Who’ll be the department rep?” Everyone votes for you, except you. Duties unspecified. Accept?
Vadik from IT says: “Your computer is about to update, but I can make it not happen.” In return he wants silence about his cat living in the server room. Your choice?
Gleb brought a box labeled “Do Not Open.” The whole department is circling it. Gleb’s in a meeting. Open it?
On a client call Gleb set his background to a beach with palm trees and surf sounds. The client asks where you all work. Your answer?
Gleb sent the department an invite to an “emergency meeting” in the cafeteria. On the table: a cake with your face on it. It’s not your birthday. Your reaction?
Eduard reviews your email to a client and adds three paragraphs “for completeness.” The client asked for a one-word answer. Keep his version?
Eduard explains how to properly cook buckwheat while you’re eating buckwheat. You’ve been cooking it for twenty years. Your reply?
Eduard fixed a bug in your code with the comment “Learn, kiddo.” The code failed tests because of his change. What do you do?
On the phone, Zoya is loudly discussing a new employee with a friend, not knowing he sits at the next desk. He’s turning red. Intervene?
A courier calls Zoya, and she answers on speakerphone for the whole office: “Leave it at the door, I’m in an important meeting!” You are the door. What do you do?
right: Tell the courier to bring it in

text: Your desk neighbor takes all personal calls on speaker “so his ear doesn’t overheat.” His grandma just asked when he’s getting married. What do you do?
Veronika keeps you after work: “Come on, I’ll show you how to properly pack documents into archive boxes.” It’ll take an hour. Go?
In the evening Stas writes: “You’re definitely coming at eight, right? I’m counting on you.” He asked you to open the office because he’ll be late. Your reply?
Gena sends a video: “Watch me do 100 push-ups. Your turn!” The team demands a response. You’re already in pajamas. What do you do?
Larisa video-calls you at 7:40 p.m. to record a voice message “while you can see me, it’s clearer that way.” Answer?
At 8 p.m. Arkady asks: “Can I book us a meeting tomorrow at 8 a.m.? It’s quick.” His “quick” is at least an hour. Agree?
Before leaving your neighbor says: “The CFO is splitting the budget tomorrow. Whisper to him that we need it more than IT.” You barely know the CFO. What do you do?
In the evening Nina Ivanovna posts in chat: “Tomorrow nobody eats lunch before 1 p.m., the gang and I have an important talk.” What about is unclear. What do you do?
Gleb leaves last and asks if he can rearrange the desks “while everyone’s asleep.” He swears it’s a prank for tomorrow. Help?
Eduard asks you to review his talk for tomorrow. It contains your ideas from last week — without mentioning you. Your move?
At 6:20 p.m. Zoya loudly calls a taxi, argues, cancels, calls again. You’re on a call with the boss. Ask her to step out?
In the evening the boss asks: “If we had to cut people, who would you keep on the team?” He expects names. Your answer?
Veronika writes: “I’ll stay late to double-check your section.” That means 30 comments on it tomorrow. What do you do?
Veronika comes in at 7:30 to align the meeting room chairs with a ruler before the day starts. Today she asks you to help “from the other end.” Help?
Veronika sent your draft to the boss with her tracked changes: 214 edits. The boss, cc’d, asks: “All good?” Reply?
Stas has prepared excuses for a whole year ahead and asks you to check for “repeats.” The list has 40 reasons; 12 are about the neighbor’s dog. What do you say?
The boss suggests you send him a list of latecomers every day at 9:05. The team would figure out who the snitch is within half a day. Agree?
Gena puts a tray of wheatgrass on the windowsill and makes you responsible for watering. You forget to water even a cactus. Take it?
This morning Gena took everyone’s blood pressure “as a precaution.” Yours is 150 over 90. Gena advises quitting coffee. Right now. What do you do?
Larisa sent a voice message from the gym: heavy breathing, clanking dumbbells and somewhere in the middle, “anyway, report by lunch.” Which report is unclear. Clarify?
Zinaida borrowed your chair “for a sec, while hers is being fixed.” It hasn’t come back for an hour. You’re working standing up. What do you do?
Arkady booked you for “Meet the New Employee.” The new employee is you. You’ve worked here three years. Go?
Arkady sent everyone a template for a “proper meeting invite” with nine mandatory fields. Your invite lacks the “emotions” field. Redo it?
IT announced: their laptop budget depends on how many departments write thank-you notes. You need a new laptop. Write one?
8:20 a.m., chat: “Who promised the boss a presentation by this morning?” You vaguely remember nodding. Confess?
Maya from HR warns: “They want to merge your department with marketing. Whoever sends the boss a plan first will run it.” Write one?
Nina Ivanovna announced she’ll no longer bake pies for the department “since nobody appreciates it.” The department is in mourning. Someone must win her over. You?
Gleb set your desktop wallpaper to your childhood photo, which he found on your social media. In 10 minutes you’re sharing your screen with a client. What do you do?
Eduard arrives before everyone and adjusts your monitor “to the correct angle.” Every morning you put it back. Today he’s waiting at your desk. What now?
At 9:15 Zoya is video-chatting with a friend in the open office at 80% volume. Everyone can see and hear the friend. Suggest headphones?
In the smoking area you heard the head of sales wants to poach your best specialist. It’s just a rumor so far. Warn your boss?
The new guy asks if it’s true that Nina Ivanovna, not the boss, runs everything here. The boss is standing two meters away. Your answer?
With a straight face, Gleb hands everyone a form: “Readiness to Relocate to the Moon.” It’s signed by HR at the bottom. You almost believed it. Fill it out?
Arkady asks you to “hold” the meeting room until he arrives. You’ve sat there alone for 20 minutes, and he isn’t answering. Keep sitting?
Veronika refuses to go to lunch until every shade of blue in the deck matches. She won’t let anyone else go either. What do you do?
Stas shows up at noon and asks you for the morning’s summary “in a nutshell.” The morning was stormy. Fill him in?
Gena organized a lunch contest: “Who can eat the most broccoli.” The winner gets a day off. In?
Larisa sent a 3-minute voice message. You listened but still can’t tell if she agrees or not. Call her back?
Zinaida drops by “just to ask,” with a report that isn’t for you. You’ve explained three times whom it’s for. What now?
Arkady is hosting a meeting on “meeting culture” and is 15 minutes late. Everyone is waiting. Someone has to start. You?
Accounting offers your department a trade: you give them your training budget, they give you the window meeting room. Your boss is on vacation. Your call.
Sales hung a “Most Useless Departments” ranking in the hallway. Yours is number two. Your response?
The boss is tearing into the department over a late report. You hear your colleague Tanya quietly crying. Tanya delayed the report. Take the hit for her?
Eduard read your chat message and replied: “It’s ‘its,’ not ‘it’s.’” You were reporting a fire in the server room. Reply?
For 25 minutes Zoya has been loudly explaining to her mom over the phone how to use a messenger app. Mom doesn’t get it. The whole office does by now. Help?
Nina Ivanovna decided your department will wear matching T-shirts to the party. The color is “up to you,” meaning pink. What do you do?
Gleb called you on the internal line imitating the CEO and asked for a “morale report” immediately. You’re already carrying it over. What next?
Vadik from IT offers you “secret” access to every manager’s calendar. You’d always know where the boss is. Take it?
An analyst from the next department asks for your data for his report and promises to “credit you.” You’ve seen his past reports: no credits. Give it?
The sixth-floor meeting room has the best view and is always empty. They say it’s cursed: every meeting there falls through. You urgently need a room. Take it?
At 10:30 p.m. Veronika writes: “Sorry for the late hour, but your file name has a space before the dot.” There is indeed a space. Reply?
Stas writes: “I finally figured out why I’m late — I’m a lark stuck on a night owl’s schedule.” He asks you to back his request for different hours. Will you?
Gena invites you to evening “partner yoga.” Your job is to hold him up in boat pose. Go?
Larisa recorded an 8-minute voice greeting and wants it sent on behalf of the department for a client’s anniversary. The audio is bad. Send it?
Zinaida catches you in the elevator at 7 p.m.: “Just a quick question — did you sign my request?” You’ve never heard of it. Promise?
Arkady booked an “Informal Get-Together” at a bar on Friday and marked it mandatory. You planned to sleep till Monday. What do you do?
7 p.m. The CFO calls an evening meeting “for an honest talk about the budget.” Your boss didn’t come, but you did. Will you speak?
Security demands you vacate the meeting room by 8 p.m., but you’re on a call with a team on the other side of the world, where it’s morning. The call just started. What now?
At 8 p.m. the boss writes: “Who got into a fight with a client today?” Two colleagues did — loudly and in front of everyone. Answer him?
The colleague you botched a project with wants to agree on who says what at the retro. His version only benefits him. Your move?
Maya from HR writes: “Could you unofficially tell me tomorrow who in the department is unhappy with the boss?” Everyone is. Reply?
Nina Ivanovna calls in the evening asking you to back her for “Employee of the Year.” In return, she promises to back you next year. What now?
Gleb invites you to film a “funny video about the department” for the office party tonight. The script mocks the boss. Will you act in it?
At a Friday dinner Eduard is teaching the waiter how to pronounce the dishes. The waiter is barely holding it together. You’re sitting next to Eduard. How do you save the evening?
By your building you overhear Zoya on the phone: “…and that new one of yours, the one always carrying a thermos.” The thermos one is you. What do you do?
You accidentally recorded a 40-second voice message to the team chat. You can hear yourself singing in the shower. Delete or keep?
Before her vacation Veronika left you an 18-page manual on watering her ficus. You open it in the evening. Read it?
Your desk neighbor closes his laptop at 6 p.m.: “Let’s hit a bar, I’ll tell you who really runs this office.” Go?
Stas sends a photo of himself running for a train, captioned: “See, I’m trying!” The train is at 6:45 p.m.; the meeting was at 5. Reply?
At 9 p.m. Gleb adds you to a chat called “Department for Fighting Arkady,” three members. Arkady is in it too. Apparently by mistake. What do you do?
7:30 p.m. The chat is debating who goes to the CEO tomorrow “for the whole department” after the blown delivery. Five people vote against you going, three for. What do you write?
At the team lunch Eduard explains to the cafeteria cook how to properly salt soup. The cook looks at you — you’re next in line. Your move?
